I’ll continue to repurchase this sunscreen because it works fabulously with my oily, acne-prone skin. It’s also helpful for my 50-something mom’s mature skin. I also converted our visual editor, Jason Speakman, into a fan—he noticed a decrease in facial redness over six months of daily use.

Neutrogena's sunscreen stick is a great product for those on the run, says Dr. Goldenberg. It's easy to apply or reapply, and it offers SPF 50 with water resistance, so people with active lifestyles really love it—just check the 10,208 perfect 5-star ratings on Amazon.

Neutrogena is cheap, travel-friendly, glides on clear, and is effective. However, we found it was too greasy for oily skin. However, if you have normal or dry skin, or just want to glow, this is the face sunscreen for you. With festival season underway, your skin will definitely “shine bright like a diamond” with the help of this sunscreen. And honestly, at just under $10, it’s worth trying.

Dr. Campbell is a fan of EltaMD's sunscreen, as are Lindsay Geller, Women's Health's lifestyle director, and Amanda Lucci, our special projects director. It contains hyaluronic acid, so Dr. Campbell often recommends it to patients with drier skin. EltaMD boasts a fragrance-free, paraben-free, and noncomedogenic formulation, making it ideal for sensitive and acne-prone skin.

The lotion has a creamy, slightly whipped texture that requires a little extra effort to blend into the skin, but it’s worth it, says Geller. However, our editors with medium to dark skin tones say this leaves a white cast on their skin, but using the Tinted version can help.

La Roche-Posay is one of the most reliable skincare brands in the game. The line is a favorite of many dermatologists I consulted, and Dr. Ranella Hirsch, MD, highlights this particular sunscreen as her top pick. She highlights the creamy formulation, which hydrates her skin and leaves it feeling velvety soft.

This is also Ritchey's new go-to. “As long as you don't smother yourself in it, I feel like it's pretty light for a sunscreen,” she says. “It's a little tacky after going on, but honestly, it was kind of nice—it definitely helped my makeup stick!” It also has a faint sunscreen smell, which she doesn't mind, since it reminds her that Anthelios Melt-In is working. She’s a self-described heavy sweater, and didn’t experience any streaking with this sunscreen.

Just keep in mind that a little goes a long way—a lesson Ritchey learned the hard way. “The first time I put too much in my hand, I looked like Larry the Lifeguard from SpongeBob SquarePants.”

Dermatologists advise applying two finger-lengths of sunscreen—about a quarter-sized amount—to your face and neck.

Read more: How Much Sunscreen You Should Use On Your Face?

Tower 28 is one of the best sunscreens that I’ve ever used. It combines all of the benefits of a broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen with foundation-like coverage in 17 shades.

It offers light-to-medium coverage that evens out my complexion without looking cakey or feeling goopy on my face. Problem spots like hyperpigmentation could use some extra love with concealer—Tower 28 makes a sweet one—but I don’t feel insecure if those spots show through with this sunscreen. It took me some trial and error to discover my exact shade, but I landed on the color 40 Silver Lake on my face and use 55 Temescal as a bronzer for a deep golden warmth.

Application is also a breeze—it applies nicely with the warmth of my fingers, but I get the most coverage when using a densely packed brush like my BK Beauty 101 Foundation Brush. I just apply the SPF to my face, buff the fluffy bristles in small, circular motions across my face, and I experience zero streaks.

Knowing that richer sunscreen shades can be a real let-down, I hit up digital designer Taryn Colbert to give this one a whirl. She uses the color 55 and puts its color payoff and longevity to the test. Tower 28 applies evenly to her bare skin and feels like nothing is on her face. Since she doesn’t have any texture or acne issues, she didn’t notice any splotches or separation with extra oil. I also have oily skin and noticed some pore emphasis on my cheeks after a few hours of wear, but honestly, touching up with oil-blotting sheets and a thin, fresh layer of SPF helps.

While Colbert and I agree with Tower 28’s sentiment that the colors are flexible, it would still be nice to have a wider range of undertones in the tan and deep shades. Still, it’s the SPF that replaces my foundation each summer and one I recommend to anyone who doesn’t want to compromise on sun protection or cosmetic coverage.

Powder sunscreen is the most underrated formulation—and Brush on Block is my favorite. It comes in a tube that features soft bristles that I dust over my face like a setting powder. It’s mess-free, making it ideal for touch-ups on the go. The broad-spectrum sunscreen is also water-resistant, so I can dust it on while poolside without worry.

But above all, it earned major snaps from Dr. King, who uses it on her face and scalp as a dry shampoo hack. Beyond perking up your hair by absorbing oil, it can add volume and texture by coating your strands with fine powders, making your hair appear fuller without sticky residue, says Dr. Goldenberg. So how should you apply it? Dr. King likes to gently rub or massage the powder into the scalp with her fingertips so that it’s not visible, she says.

The only downside? There is only one shade available: Translucent. It hasn’t left my caramel complexion looking ghostly. However, the brand makes other tinted powder sunscreens. I’d appreciate it if this SPF 50 became available in richer shades to accommodate more melanin-rich complexions and anyone with dark hair like mine.

Although it’s expensive, associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz has repurchased this sunscreen for over three years. ColoreScience is the only tinted sunscreen Zitz found that matches her cool-toned fair complexion without leaning too warm or too dark. “Tinted or non-tinted, it’s one of the only sunscreens that doesn’t cause acne—and I’m on Accutane—and it feels really nice on my skin,” she says.

Men’s Health associate health and fitness editor Jocelyn Solis-Moreira found success with the shade Medium. She admits being picky about sunscreens and often stocks up on European and Asian brands when traveling because those typically don’t leave behind a dreaded whitecast. However, ColoreScience impressed her after one try.

“With only a pea-sized amount, I saw an immediate difference in my face,” she says. It helped brighten her complexion, masked redness on her nose, and even had friends complimenting her glow. “It honestly felt like a layer of foundation that blended perfectly into my tan skin,” she says. She was so delighted with the results that she didn’t even apply concealer or setting powder. “I had to honestly do a double-take the first time that I was applying sunscreen and not makeup,” she says. “I would 100% recommend this product and will be a regular customer after this experience.”

Colbert was impressed by the lightweight texture but noted it required more effort to use. Notably, she had to wait for it to transform from white to her rich complexion before blending it onto her face. Colbert admits she had to work the sunscreen into her skin to ensure it didn’t look streaky, and that she didn’t miss any spots while waiting for the color to change. Still, she appreciates the overall appearance it left on her complexion. While not her perfect shade match, rich does resemble how her skin looks after a beach vacation.

Although each shade adapts to your complexion, I passed on this one because the limited color range wasn't a good fit for my olive undertones. Still, given the multiple rave reviews from our staff, it’s worth trying if you have the extra funds.

The world of sunscreen can sometimes feel like a catch-22: Either you're stuck using SPF that imparts a gnarly white cast, or you're using one that leaves your skin irritated and sensitive. The Supergoop! PLAY Everyday Lotion with SPF 50 sidesteps both of those issues, according to editorial assistant Katie Mogg. “The lightweight formula melts into my skin seamlessly, all while making it feel hydrated and nourished,” she says. Plus, it offers 80 minutes of water resistance, making it her go-to SPF for my sweaty outdoor running sessions.

Although I prefer a tinted face sunscreen, when I know I’ll be near the water or exercising outdoors I opt for this SPF. Play Everyday is my beach bag essential and for any trips to the park. It absorbs quickly without leaving behind a sticky residue on my body. Supergoop! doesn’t leave behind an ashy finish either. Instead, it blends flawlessly into my complexion.

The only thing I’d change about this sunscreen is the sizing options. There are four sizes, the most of any recommendations this list. However, only the extra large 18 fl. oz bottle comes with a pump. It would be nice to have the flexability of a pump with the other sizes, or at least the standard. But it’s not a true deal breaker, and I still like how slim the original squeeze bottle of sunscreen is and how it doesn’t take up too much space in my checked suitcase and beach bag.

Supergoop! is a favorite among dermatologists and our editors for its super-clear formulas—and rightfully so! This all-over version of the brand's star product—the Unseen Sunscreen SPF 40—does the same thing its predecessor does: it goes on invisible, feels velvety and weightless, and offers out-of-this-world sun protection.

"So many sunscreens have given my skin this heavy, greasy feeling right after I apply them, and on a really hot day in the sun, sometimes that can make you feel even hotter," says beauty contributor Danielle Jackson. "This formula is so light that I almost forgot I even had it on. It really makes you feel like you're not wearing anything."

Aloian has oily skin and easily breaks out, but she didn’t experience any body acne with this SPF. She didn't layer it with other body products, but she was impressed by how easily it spread, thanks to its more liquid texture, which blends into her sensitive areas like the neck. “I love this sunscreen—it doesn't leave any white streaks or irritate my skin. It'll definitely stay in my skincare routine for the long haul,” she says.

Honestly, the only con with this sunscreen is that it’s slightly pricey. However, we’ve been testing this SPF for over a month, and our editors predict each container will last them two to three months before a restock.

Ultraviolet radiation from the sun falls into two categories: ultraviolet A (UVA) and ultraviolet B (UVB). UVA rays cause signs of aging, such as hyperpigmentation, lines, and wrinkles. Meanwhile, UVB rays can cause more serious damage, including sunburn and skin cancer. Your safest bet is to only use broad-spectrum sunscreens to help protect against UVA and UVB rays.

Next, choose either a mineral or a chemical sunscreen. Here’s more insight to help you determine between the two formulations.

They both have benefits and limitations, but ultimately, the best one is the sunscreen you’ll actually use and reapply. As for me? Well, I like both types. However, I typically use mineral sunscreen on my face, so I can head outside immediately after work instead of lingering for the approximately 15-minute waiting period associated with chemical sunscreens.

Broad-spectrum coverage, sunscreen type, and SPF coverage are the big three considerations. But another factor worth emphasizing is other non-active skincare ingredients that will help bolster your complexion. Dermatologist Elyse Love, MD, is a big fan of niacinamide to calm the skin and improve its tone and texture. Also, look for ingredients that support your skin type and goals. For example, if you want to brighten your complexion, you'll look for a sunscreen with vitamin C. If you have dry skin, seek out hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid.

When we initially published this story in May 2019, it was a gallery featuring a handful of sunscreens. Nearly seven years later, we’ve seriously upgraded our product vetting process.

For starters, we polled dermatologists about the actual sunscreens they use IRL and recommend to patients. The doctors answered a series of questions about the efficacy, application, and real-world testing experience that helped inform their suggestions.

Next, I evaluated the hundreds of sunscreens in the Women’s Health beauty closet. I also polled Women’s Health and Men’s Health editors about their ride-or-die sunscreens. Our team varies across age, skin type, complexion, budget, and lifestyle. For example, fitness editor Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor. She has a no-frills approach to beauty and wants a simple sunscreen that delivers results, which she found in La Roche-Posay.

Clear sunscreens were carefully evaluated. Our team asked ourselves if the clear sunscreens squeezed out clear or were they white or creamy and then blended out without a trace? Associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian and editorial assistant Katie Mogg found success with Supergoop!

Tinted sunscreens were also inspected because I know firsthand what it’s like to try and find your best color match only for it to look ruddy or cool in natural sunlight. With 17 flexible shades, Tower 28 delivers the most inclusive range among the sunscreens we vetted. The hues vary in depth and undertone, and offer light-to-medium coverage.

Whether you have oily, dry, or combination skin, there's something on our list for you. Meet our team’s all-time favorite sunscreens that we’ll continue to rely on throughout 2026.

You’ll want to keep an eye out for certain key phrases on the label. Dealing with sensitive skin? Dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum, MD, recommends fragrance-free and hypoallergenic formulas. She also prefers mineral sunscreens made with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide for sensitive skin because they’re less likely to cause irritation. Acne happens to the best of us, but your best path forward is to use an oil-free and non-comedogenic sunscreen that won’t congest your pores.

#4895. Boris Johnson says UK must lead blockchain development despite crypto doubts

Johnson was joined by Lord Ross Kempsell who called for regulators to work with industry participants to bring the UK to the forefront.

Former United Kingdom Prime Minister Boris Johnson has backed blockchain technology and tokenization as opportunities for the UK’s financial sector, despite persistent doubts about cryptocurrencies.

Speaking at Solana’s Breakpoint conference in London on Monday, Johnson maintained his position that Bitcoin (BTC) resembles a Ponzi scheme, following an opinion piece published in the Daily Mail in March. He questioned who investors could hold accountable if funds were stolen.

However, Johnson distinguished his criticism of digital assets from his view of the underlying technology, saying the UK should be at the forefront of tokenization.

Lord Ross Kempsell, who joined Johnson on stage, said although he shared his reservations on cryptocurrencies, “on the parts of the industry that can be brought into a regulated perimeter, which the regulators are working on, there’s a lot of scope here for a high growth industry.”

Kempsell, whom Johnson nominated for a peerage in 2022, told the panel that more than 8% of UK adults hold crypto, in line with Financial Conduct Authority-commissioned research published in December 2025. Speaking to Cointelegraph after his stage appearance, he said, “I’m a very big believer in making London and keeping London as the onchain capital for innovation.”

Related: UK financial watchdog opens consultations for DeFi guidance, crypto laws

He argued that consumer protection and financial innovation should not be treated as competing priorities, pointing to the UK’s established fintech industry as an example of how regulation can coexist with innovation in the country. He said the UK should avoid introducing a single, all-encompassing piece of crypto legislation, opting instead for “a more ad-hoc approach” to regulation.

He called for collaboration between the regulators and market participants to understand both the risks and opportunities. While he saw consumer protection as “paramount,” he felt it was unfair to single out the crypto industry as the only sector where consumer protection was at risk.

“Really what I care about is the economic growth potential that there is in this industry, the job creation potential, and also its wider links to tech, AI and traditional financial innovation. London’s always been at the center of those historically,” Kempsell told Cointelegraph.

When asked about the approach of the current administration in the UK, he highlighted that “they need to make sure that they get the fundamental market conditions right.” In his eyes, that meant making the UK a competitive player in regard to tax and facilitating business innovation.

Related: UK names 6 banks to lead first digitally native government bond

Tim Meggs, co-founder of London-based digital asset trading firm Lo:Tech, said Johnson “made a fair point about people getting burned,” but said most of the losses experienced by the industry stemmed from thin liquidity and a lack of visibility over how prices were made.

“If the FCA gets its perimeter right, the UK has a chance to make that kind of transparency the norm,” Meggs said. “But until the clearing and prime broking infrastructure catches up, good rules won’t be enough on their own to make London the place where serious digital asset trading gets done.”

Robin Nordnes, founder and CEO of Solana infrastructure firm Raiku, argued that Johnson’s question about who is in charge makes the case for blockchain, since a public ledger needs no guarantor. “Every transaction on Solana is public and can be checked by anyone, which is more than you can say for most of what happens in the City,” he said.

Nordnes warned that “if Westminster keeps treating this as retail speculation, the trading systems behind the next generation of markets will be built in New York and Singapore, and London will end up renting them.”

#4893. Hackers Redirected Bitcoin Miner Rewards via AI Attack, Luxor CEO Says

Hackers Redirected Bitcoin Miner Rewards via AI Attack, Luxor CEO Says

Hackers briefly hijacked computing power from Bitcoin miners using Luxor’s fleet management software, in what the company’s CEO called an AI-enabled attack.

Luxor Technology said Sunday that its internal monitoring flagged an unauthorized redirect of hashrate through Commander, its tool for managing mining machines.

Hashrate is the computing power miners devote to securing Bitcoin and earning rewards. Just over a dozen client accounts were affected, with their machines pointed to a different mining pool for a limited window, effectively sending the value of their work elsewhere.

Luxor said it patched Commander within two hours and began restoring affected machines to their original settings. No data was leaked or taken from its systems, and the issue was isolated to Commander, according to the company.

Luxor Pool and its LuxOS software weren’t affected, the company said, adding that every affected client will be paid in full for the redirected hashrate, as if their machines had mined normally.

Luxor CEO Nick Hansen said the compromise began around 6 p.m. Pacific time Saturday through “a sophisticated AI-enabled vector.” He didn’t detail how the attack worked. “You trust us with your fleet, and we need to be better,” he wrote on X.

Around 6:00p PDT yesterday, a subset of Commander customers were compromised, through a sophisticated AI-enabled vector. We were able to identify and patch quickly so that it didn't continue, then the hard work of reverting started.…

In a follow-up post, Hansen said crypto businesses are now “inundated with AI-enabled attacks,” with abliterated models, or AI models stripped of their safety guardrails, probing systems around the clock for weaknesses.

Luxor has responded by buying its own bare-metal GPUs to run such models defensively. It has also put most new feature work on hold to harden its infrastructure by rotating keys, updating kernels and pinning dependencies. Hansen urged other companies running similar services to do the same.

Bitcoin developers are grappling with the same threat. Bitcoin Core updated its security policy to address AI-driven threats, and an AI “red team” effort has turned up critical vulnerabilities throughout the year.

The incident also follows other attacks on Bitcoin infrastructure. Blockstream’s Liquid Network restored full Bitcoin backing earlier this month, two months after a $320 million exploit.

Luxor said it would soon publish a full post-mortem of the hack.

#4892. Bitmine edges toward 5% of ETH supply as treasuries report buys amid market slump

Strategy, Strive, Bitmine and Cypherpunk disclosed fresh additions to their crypto treasuries, spanning Bitcoin, Ether and Zcash.

Publicly traded crypto treasury companies Bitmine, Strive and Cypherpunk Technologies disclosed increases in their cryptocurrency holdings on Monday, joining Strategy in accumulating digital assets despite a broader market downturn.

Bitmine, the largest publicly traded Ether treasury company, said it added 7,653 Ether (ETH) over the past week, bringing its total holdings to 6.08 million ETH, about 4.97% of its total supply and bringing it ever closer to its stated aim of accumulating 5% of the ETH supply, according to a Monday announcement.

Top Bitcoin treasury companies Strategy and Strive also reported purchases. Strategy acquired 485 Bitcoin (BTC) for $33.4 million, while Strive bought 251 BTC for $17.5 million, bringing its holdings to 43,404 BTC — just 110 BTC behind Twenty One Capital, the third-largest publicly traded Bitcoin holder, according to BitcoinTreasuries.net data.

Zcash (ZEC) treasury and mining company Cypherpunk Technologies reported buying 3,775.72 ZEC for $3.48 million since September and mining another 5,721.35 ZEC in October. The additions brought its holdings to 341,858.75 ZEC, or around 2% of circulating supply.

The purchases come amid a broader cryptocurrency sell-off. Bitcoin was trading around $65,017, down 12.9% over the past seven days and 20% over the past month. ETH fell 14.2% and ZEC dropped 22.9% over the past week, according to CoinGecko data as of 8:08 pm UTC on Monday.

Bitcoin is down around 20% over the past month. Source: CoinGecko

#4890. The 8 Best Slippers for Women for Max Coziness, Tested By a Style Writer

From couch-rotting to errands, these kicks have you covered.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Now that the weather has cooled down and leaves are on the ground, my style writer brain is in peak outfit mode. I’ve already imagined the ways I’ll wear my leather jackets, chunky knits, and bootcut jeans. But before I start styling my way through the fall and winter, there’s one essential I always reach for first: slippers. I test a lot of shoes in the name of journalism, and few spark more joy than a pair of cute slippers that add the perfect cozy feel to any outfit. Whether I’m channeling my inner couch potato on a lazy Sunday or running errands around town, the best slippers in my stash hit the sweet spot of soft, supportive, and actually stylish.

A lot of the same principles that apply to shopping for supportive sneakers also apply to slippers, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX. After all, a slipper is the ultimate cozy shoe, but it’s also incredibly useful for keeping your arches happy while walking around hardwood floors at home. That’s why Sharkey says cushioning and arch support are key. Your slippers should feel plush underfoot, but not so squishy that you lose stability. Where you plan to wear them also matters: A pair of house slippers needs less traction and durability than a pair for outdoors, which should have a thicker, more grippy bottom.

After over a year of testing, I found slippers that are plush enough to lounge in, supportive enough for a spin around town, and stylish enough that you’ll actually want to wear them.

When it comes to a slipper that checks every box (plush, supportive, and legitimately stylish), the Ugg Cozy Slipper is the one I always come back to. I’ve been wearing this slipper since fall 2024 with everything from jeans and Henleys to matching sweat sets.

The slipper earns its name with extra-cozy materials, from the sheepskin fur lining to the sweater-knit outer and fluffy collar. I love that it keeps my feet warm and toasty, even during cold winter months. Board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bobby Pourizaee, DPM says this slipper is excellent for comfort and lounging. Podiatrist and board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bruce Pinker, DPM agrees, adding that the slip-on style makes this slipper easy to wear.

Beneath the fluff, there’s real structure that keeps my feet fatigue-free. The contoured footbed and firm-yet-plush midsole made with 17 mm of sheepskin hug my arches just right. The outsole is sturdy and grippy, made with dense EVA foam and tons of traction. I wear it on long walks with my dog around the Long Island suburbs and never worry about slipping or falling, no matter the weather. However, it’s still lightweight enough to feel like an indoor slipper.

Pinker says that it could be improved if the heel region were closed for more support and stability, but the easy-on, easy-off fit is part of why I love this slipper. If you’re after something warm, cozy, and super stylish for both indoor and outdoor wear, I can’t recommend this slipper enough.

For a cozy, budget-friendly slipper that doesn’t skimp on comfort, the Dearfoams Lacey Memory Foam Slipper is the one I’ve been living in lately. At under $30, this slipper is way more cushy, warm, and supportive than lots of other house slippers I’ve worn.

I padded around my house in this slipper nonstop for about a year, and it held up beautifully through coffee runs to the kitchen, long hours at my desk, and quick trips to grab packages. It’s definitely a house slipper, but in the best way possible—pure comfort, with just enough structure to feel supportive.

The memory foam cushioning is what makes this slipper so comfortable, Sharkey says. Each step in it feels super plush, molding to the shape of my foot for that “walking on pillows” feel. The fleece lining also keeps my feet cozy without overheating, and the soft knit upper gives it a lounge-all-day kind of vibe that pairs perfectly with pajamas and sweatpants. I absolutely love the heel and arch cushioning, especially when my feet ache after a long day commuting to and from Manhattan, but Sharkey says they should only be worn in the house since they lack the structure needed for long periods on your feet.

But for a house slipper, there’s way more support than I expected. The raised heel area keeps the slipper from sliding off my foot, even when I’m walking up or down stairs. It’s a small but thoughtful feature that makes it feel a bit more secure than your average slip-on. And while the outsole isn’t meant for outdoor adventures, it’s durable enough for quick steps onto the porch or grabbing the mail.

I wore this slipper for nearly a year straight while trodding around my house, and absolutely love them. However, I will say that at about the 10-month mark, they needed to be replaced, as they stretched out a bit and lost some of the much-needed cushioning, support, and traction.

Thanks to its incredible level of cushioning, the Vionic Gemma II Mule Slipper keeps my feet pain-free even after walking in it all day. Pourizaee says it's a strong recommendation thanks to the contoured footbed. The midsole is made from a flexible EVA foam that not only feels super plush under my foot but is designed to absorb shock and reduce stress on the joints. I have lingering ankle and foot pain on one side from a previous high ankle sprain, and while some shoes exacerbate those symptoms, this slipper keeps my feet happy. That comes as no surprise, since this slipper earned an APMA Seal of Acceptance.

It also has great support and stability features. Pinker says it would be improved with a closed-heel design, but I find that the deep heel cup helps, and the strap closure keeps my foot firmly planted—even while speed walking on city sidewalks. Pourizaee adds that the contoured footbed helps keep feet aligned and relieves foot strain. While I often wake up with sore feet that hurt as soon as I step out of bed, I find that when I’ve worn this slipper the day before, foot fatigue is next to zero.

If you like a cozy slipper, the Gemma II delivers. I have the cream color, which is made with a wool upper that keeps my feet warm and looks cute with all my cold-weather loungewear. Other styles have a faux-fur or flannel upper, which also looks super warm and cozy. Plus, since the slipper is designed for indoor and outdoor wear, the synthetic outsole is ultra-durable with a patterned tread design. I’ve even gone for post-rain walks with my dog on wet pavement, and never felt like I was going to slip.

Overall, this slipper is warm, cozy, and ultra-cushioned. It keeps my feet happy with the plush feel underfoot, and I love keeping it by the door when I need a cute shoe to slip on fast.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The Ortho-Cushion system (which includes the removable orthotic insole, ergonomic sole, and fitting spacers) helps to customize the fit and level of cushioning and support. I didn’t realize before selecting my normal size that Orthofeet recommends ordering a half-size down for a more snug fit, but placing the smallest blue fitting spacer (1/16 inch) under the insole kept my foot feeling super secure. Even without any customization, I was impressed by the high level of cushioning that hugs my arches and feels really nice under my heels. The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. Sharkey says it's a good cozy and comfortable option, and that Bombas did a great job with the level of cushioning. That’s thanks to the memory foam footbed, which has a nice squishy feel, contours to the shape of the foot, and softens impact with every step. That contouring feature does wonders for making sure the slipper stays on, even while trekking all around town. However, Sharkey says the backless design does tend to slip off the feet if you’re not careful. I haven’t had any issues there, but it’s something to keep in mind if your feet need an ultra-supportive shoe—in which case, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper might be a better choice.

The rubber outsole gives this slip-on shoe a major upgrade, since it helps provide traction when I wear it outside. I keep this slipper mainly for wearing around the house or quick errands, but I have worn it during short, casual walks without worry. The fluffy sherpa material, inside and out, makes it a super cozy option for lazy days cuddled up on the couch and keeps my feet warm even when I take it for a spin outdoors.

Plus, there’s plenty of chic color options. I went with the cream, which I find pairs well with almost anything in my closet—but there’s also a black and brown for additional neutrals, and a dusty purple or tomato red option for something more bold. Clogs get a bad rap for making your feet sweat, slide around, and (sorry!) being kind of ugly. But this slip-on clog from Rothy’s nails it on the style front, and is also durable, breathable, and super comfortable. The Casual Clog is well-loved by me and executive editor Abigail Cuffey—oh, and Sharkey recommends it, too.

She wears it as a lounge shoe and an outdoor shoe, because of the grippy outsole and substantial feel. Cuffey’s thoughts on the merino wool clog are generally the same, but she loves that the wool feels a little cozier while still airy and breathable. “I usually go through slippers so fast because they get so gross, but Rothy’s Casual Clogs are the first ones that have staying power in my closet,” she says.

#4888. Bitcoin's $2 Billion Liquidation Weekend Leaves Traders Watching $60,000

Bitcoin's $2 Billion Liquidation Weekend Leaves Traders Watching $60,000

Bitcoin fell to around $62,100 on Sunday as roughly $2 billion in crypto derivatives positions were forcibly closed, mostly bets that prices would rise. The weekend slide sent the cryptocurrency to its lowest level since July 14, adding another ugly chapter to six consecutive weeks of losses.

Bitcoin had recovered to around $64,300 early Monday. But the options market is showing why traders aren't necessarily treating that bounce as an all-clear.

Liquidations happen when an exchange closes a trader's position because the money posted to support a borrowed bet is no longer enough to cover its losses. CoinGlass figures from Saturday showed $1.9 billion liquidated in one 24-hour period, about $1.8 billion of it bullish positions across cryptocurrencies, not just Bitcoin.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had already been losing investors before the weekend. Data from Decrypt’s ETF tracker show $185.4 million in net outflows on Friday, extending their losing streak to seven trading sessions and bringing withdrawals since November 5 to approximately $1.91 billion.

BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $143.5 million of Friday's withdrawals, while Fidelity's FBTC lost $41.9 million. The funds' earlier weakness had helped explain the broader exodus, although ETF flow totals measure fund creations and redemptions rather than every trade between investors.

Those numbers also come with a timing distinction: U.S. ETFs do not trade over the weekend, while Bitcoin trades around the clock. Friday's outflows show weakened demand before the crash, not that ETF shareholders were redeeming shares during Sunday's plunge.

Bitcoin's technical indicators suggest the selling may be overstretched, but that doesn't necessarily mean the worst is over.

The daily Relative Strength Index sat near 24 in oversold territory on the daily charts. Meanwhile, the Average Directional Index stood above 33, indicating a strong prevailing trend, with bearish directional pressure still dominating. The weekly RSI, near 38, pointed to a weak longer-term picture, although it had not reached oversold territory.

The cryptocurrency bounced after approaching support around $62,000. A recovery would face potential resistance near $66,500 to $67,200, followed by another obstacle around $69,300, based on the chart's Fibonacci levels that measure support and resistance marks.

A decisive break below $62,000, meanwhile, would put the psychologically important $60,000 level back in focus—precisely where options traders have accumulated significant downside exposure.

Bitcoin's next test will be whether fresh U.S. ETF flow data show more withdrawals for Monday and whether traders keep paying for downside protection. The heavily watched November 27 options expiration is still ahead, with $50,000 puts among the contracts drawing the most recent trading activity.

#4887. Binance hack may push institutions to outside custody, FalconX exec says

FalconX’s Joshua Lim says the Binance hack could push institutions to keep crypto off exchanges and change how large investors trade in 2027.

A major shift in institutional crypto trading could be on the horizon following the recent Binance hack, as security concerns may lead to more large investors keeping their assets outside exchanges, according to a FalconX executive.

In an exclusive interview with Cointelegraph at the Digital Asset Forum in New York City on Nov. 13, Joshua Lim, global head of markets at FalconX, a digital asset brokerage for institutional investors, said the Oct. 29 hack could make institutions more cautious about trading crypto and change how they store their assets.

“It’s actually quite bearish for more institutional participation in crypto,” Lim told Cointelegraph. He said traders initially played down the hack but later began to recognize its potential long-term impact.

As a result, Lim expects more institutions to turn to outside custody providers and trading firms that allow them to trade without keeping their crypto on exchanges, a shift he believes could become one of the biggest trends in 2027.

North Korean-linked hackers stole about $6.4 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, making it the largest crypto theft on record, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

The shift toward keeping crypto outside exchanges already appeared to be underway even before the hack. In an October proposal, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said industry practices were developing that reduced the need to move investment advisers’ client assets and regulated funds’ crypto holdings out of permitted custody for trading.

Lim pointed to Copper, a crypto custody provider, as one company that could benefit. Its ClearLoop service lets investors trade on supported exchanges while keeping their crypto with a separate company.

Copper said collateral protected by its ClearLoop service supported more than $240 billion in perpetual futures trading volume during the first quarter of 2026, more than double the amount a year earlier.

Lim explained that investors can keep their assets outside an exchange while receiving credited balances that allow them to trade on it. Under the brokerage model Lim described, a hedge fund can place trades through FalconX, which executes them using its own exchange accounts and relationships. Still, investors face risks tied to the firms holding their assets and settling their trades.

“For many players, facing a regulated entity like ours is more palatable,” Lim added.

Related: Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

Binance recorded large Bitcoin outflows in mid-November, although it is not clear whether they were linked to the hack.

According to CryptoQuant data, Binance recorded net withdrawals of about 2,771 Bitcoin (BTC) on Friday, followed by 2,708 BTC on Saturday and 5,636 BTC on Sunday — totaling about 11,115 BTC leaving the exchange than entered over those three days.

The withdrawals came as the broader crypto market was falling, with Bitcoin trading around $65,000 at 9:41 pm UTC Monday, down about 20% over the past month, according to CoinGecko.

However, the data does not show who moved the Bitcoin or why. Investors could have transferred their funds to personal wallets, companies that store crypto on their behalf, or to other exchanges.

Beyond concerns about exchange security, Lim expects other changes in how large investors trade in 2027. He said institutions want more ways to trade assets such as oil, gold and stock market indexes through crypto platforms, including outside regular market hours.

“You can respond quickly to news events when they happen,” Lim said, citing one of the benefits of 24/7 trading.

That type of trading is already taking place on Hyperliquid, a decentralized trading platform that offers contracts tied to traditional assets. As of Monday, Hyperliquid’s markets for traditional assets and other contracts had about $4.3 billion in open interest and recorded $3.9 billion in trading volume over 24 hours, according to data from Perpys.

But while crypto platforms are giving investors more ways to trade, Lim said the financial services needed to support those trades have not kept up, particularly when it comes to borrowing money and managing risk.

For example, investors can now trade oil through traditional futures markets, investment funds and crypto platforms. But lenders may treat trades on each platform separately, even when those trades balance each other out.

“There’s not enough players that can give you leverage or margin financing against all of these things collectively,” Lim said. “The risk netting is not quite there yet.”

#4884. Bitcoin Wallet Maker Trezor Says Customer Data Was Exposed Again

Bitcoin Wallet Maker Trezor Says Customer Data Was Exposed Again

The “days since last third-party breach” counter at Trezor has reset to zero once again.

This time, hackers accessed shipping partner Skladon's systems and likely exported information tied to approximately 27,000 hardware-wallet orders, according to a company disclosure published Monday.

The intrusion occurred November 7, but Skladon did not notify Trezor until November 15. The exposed records cover orders placed between August 9 and November 7, including customers' full names, phone numbers, delivery and email addresses, plus the products they bought and their prices.

Trezor said its own systems were not compromised, and no wallet backups, PINs or passphrases were involved. The breach does not, by itself, let an attacker move a buyer's coins, but it gives them a potentially dangerous combination: a home address and evidence that someone bought a device designed to store crypto.

The latest incident follows an August shipping partner hack and a September email provider breach, making three separate third-party security incidents in a little over three months.

Trezor said some customers have already reported fraudulent phone calls. Criminals could cite the exact model and price of a wallet to make an unsolicited call, text or letter seem legitimate, or use a home address to identify someone who may hold cryptocurrency.

In August, logistics provider ShipMonk suffered a breach that initially appeared to affect fewer than 14,000 Trezor customers. An updated investigation uncovered records for another 67,000 U.S. buyers from 2019 to 2021 that ShipMonk had retained despite assurances they had been deleted, bringing the total to 80,689 people.

September brought another incident, this time at marketing email provider Brevo. Hackers used Trezor's legitimate email channel to distribute a fake security warning urging recipients to install an app that requested their wallet backups. Trezor later said 347,149 email addresses had been exported.

These weren't Trezor's first brushes with the problem. A Mailchimp insider attack targeted Trezor users in 2022, and a 2024 breach of its external support portal put the contact details of up to 66,000 people at risk.

The fallout can go beyond inbox spam. In February, fake letters were sent to hardware-wallet owners, complete with Trezor branding, holograms and QR codes leading to phishing sites.

Asked why an order from Trezor's official store involved an outside company, Trezor responded that it’s basically a logistics question, not a tech issue. “Companies of our size and global reach can’t run efficiently without third-party service providers,” the company replied to a comment on X.

Hi, companies of our size and global reach can’t run efficiently without third-party service providers. Handling as much as possible internally is the goal, but doing every part of the business ourselves isn’t realistic. Skladon is one of the partners that delivers Trezor orders,…

It said Skladon held only the information needed to deliver parcels, and handling every stage of global distribution in-house was not realistic.

Trezor says Skladon does not ship to the United States, so American buyers were not affected by this incident. Affected customers have been notified where possible, though some people who ordered between August 9 and 14 may not receive an email because Trezor had already anonymized their records.

The company has introduced anonymous pickup at parcel lockers or collection points in 18 European countries, allowing buyers to avoid supplying a home address. It is also working to shorten retention of order data from 90 to 45 days and says shipping partners will have to follow the same policy.

Trezor advises customers to ignore unexpected calls and messages about their orders, check any concerns through its official support site and never share a wallet backup. It has notified a data protection authority, but has not yet disclosed how attackers got into Skladon's systems.

#4882. WNBA Star Gabby Williams Found a Team That Asked What She Wanted. Then She Won a Championship

The 30-year-old shares her philosophy on work-life balance and how she keeps her body strong and healthy on a new episode of The Huddle.

WNBA superstar Gabby Williams is proof that hard work and persistence pay off. Drafted into the league in 2018 by the Chicago Sky, the 30-year-old has been slowly building her résumé ever since—both stateside and abroad—notching her first EuroLeague championship in 2022 with Hungary’s Sopron Basket, being named a WNBA All-Star in 2025, and, finally, winning a WNBA Championship in 2026 with the Golden State Valkyries. (She was named Finals MVP too.)

Yes, 2026 has been a big year for the forward, and she has only a couple more months to rest up before taking on her next challenge: debuting in the Unrivaled league, as part of the Miami-based Laces BC.

“It's three-on-three, so you can't hide,” Gabby tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “The positive feedback that I've heard from people who have done it, [is] that the personal development side is great. Players usually go on to have great W seasons after doing Unrivaled.”

How could Gabby possibly top this past year!? We’ll have to wait to find out, but in the meantime, she opens up about finding a home with the Valkyries, keeping herself healthy and injury-free, and building a life outside of basketball.

Over the years, Gabby has earned the nickname “the French Army knife,” due not only to her dual-citizenship (her dad is American; her mom is French) but also to her versatility on the court.

Her role on many teams has been defined by what the team needed, whether it was creating opportunities or defending the paint. But when she went into free agency and signed with the Valkyries earlier this year, it was the first time Gabby recalls someone in the league asking what she wanted to do.

“I was proud to do whatever the team needed,” Gabby says. “But it was nice to trust myself.” That trust—both in herself and from her team—has obviously paid off. Not only does Gabby say she feels more like herself than she ever has, but she has the championship (the Valkyries’ first) to show for it.

Given how little downtime Gabby takes—she often spends part of her off-season playing abroad—she’s crafted a wellness routine that prioritizes stretching, mobility, and maintenance to keep her body in peak physical condition.

And it starts first thing when she wakes up. “I'm a big foam-roller stretcher, especially as I'm getting older,” she says. “I'll spend a good like 20, 15 minutes first thing in the morning just doing my mobility stuff so that when I come to the gym my body's awake and ready.”

At the gym, Gabby and her trainers prioritize accessory work over big Olympic lifts, to limit the wear and tear on her body.

In the off-season, Gabby shifts from a maintenance mindset to an improvement focus with her workouts. If she wants to strengthen a particular body part or movement pattern (like being more explosive) this is when she has the time and energy to do it.

No matter her training regimen, Gabby ends her day much like she starts it—with recovery. She loves an epsom salt bath and can’t get enough of her Normatec compression therapy.

It might be surprising to hear a WNBA champion say “basketball is not life,” but that’s precisely Gabby’s philosophy when it comes to balancing her priorities.

“I think that's why I've been able to have so much success in basketball is because I've learned how to compartmentalize,” she says. She credits that mindset to the coaching team at the University of Connecticut, where she played in college.

“Coach said, ‘When you're on the court, I want you to be focused. I don't want you to be thinking about school. I don't want you to be thinking about your personal life. So while you're doing your other stuff, don't focus on basketball as much. Find the time for your school. When you're going out, go out, have fun.’”

And so Gabby does just that, whether it’s solving a puzzle or picking up a new book. “It is just the perfect way to consume your mind with something else,” she says of reading. She’s even started a Valkyries book club, but it got a bit sidetracked by, of all things, the playoffs. Luckily, there’s always the 2027 season to start anew.

To hear more from Gabby, including her undying love of figure skating and how she’s upped her style game, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#4881. German lawmakers back crypto freezes outside criminal cases

Customs authorities could hold “suspicious” assets for 30 days under the bill, with court oversight for extensions and disputed confiscation.

Germany’s lower house of parliament has passed a bill that would let customs authorities temporarily freeze cryptocurrency and other high-value assets suspected of having unlawful origins without first opening a criminal investigation.

The Bundestag passed the customs reform bill on Friday as part of a wider effort to combat money laundering and organized crime. The proposed procedure would target assets worth more than 100,000 euros and explicitly mentions cryptocurrencies.

Under the bill’s text approved by lawmakers, authorities would be able to hold assets for up to 30 days where there are factual indications of unlawful origins, according to a translated version. However, filing an application for confiscation could suspend those deadlines pending a court decision, and in contested cases, a court would have to be satisfied that the assets were of unlawful origin before ordering confiscation, effectively putting the burden of proof on the crypto holder.

German Social Democratic Party lawmaker Ingo Vogel said that the powers would allow authorities to pursue suspicious assets even when there are not yet grounds to open a criminal case, according to the Bundestag’s summary of the debate on the bill.

The bill still requires consent from the Bundesrat, Germany’s upper house of parliament, and is intended to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Germany’s Federal Bar Association, known as BRAK, previously opposed the government’s draft in an Oct. 28 statement, warning that the meaning of unlawful origin is too vague and risks treating missing records as evidence of illicit wealth.

The association pointed to assets inherited through generations as one example where owners may lack a paper trail. It also questioned what the administrative process would add to Germany’s existing criminal confiscation rules.

German blockchain industry association Bundesblock also raised concerns about the treatment of digital assets in a March 31 submission on an earlier draft. It warned at the time that blockchain analysis should not automatically be treated as proof of ownership or control, and that incorrect wallet attribution could even infringe fundamental rights.

Related: Crypto adoption blooming in Germany, while UK is falling ‘behind,’ says CoinShares researcher

Germany has already carried out large crypto seizures under existing law. As Cointelegraph reported, Saxony authorities sold 49,858 Bitcoin (BTC) linked to the Movie2k piracy investigation in 2024, raising about 2.6 billion euros, or $2.8 billion. At the time, prosecutors said the proceeds remained secured pending a court ruling on confiscation.

In a recent development, local outlet MDR reported on Friday that a Leipzig judge proposed ending proceedings against the main defendant in exchange for 40,000 BTC and a payment of 38 million euros for the potential victims. The proposal remains under consideration.

#4880. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max Leads China's AI Agent Race—But You Can't Download It

Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max Leads China's AI Agent Race—But You Can't Download It

Alibaba released Qwen 4 Max on Monday, its most powerful AI model yet and the first flagship built on its new Qwen 4 architecture.

It is also the highest-ranked Chinese model on Arena's agent leaderboard, putting the company ahead of Tencent, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek in that particular test.

The new model has 2.4 trillion parameters, can process text, images and video, and accepts up to one million tokens of context. Parameters are all the different dials a model can handle and tweak when processing information. Tokens are basically the smallest unit of information a model can handle. Its current configuration is enough room for lengthy codebases or stacks of documents.

Alibaba uses a mixture-of-experts design, which keeps most of those parameters idle for any given word it processes. Qwen 4 Max activates 71 billion at a time, compared with 95 billion for Qwen 3.8 Max, allowing a very large model to use less computing power per token.

On Agent Arena, Qwen 4 Max placed 14th among individual models and made Alibaba the fifth-ranked laboratory overall.

The leaderboard evaluates real agent sessions using task completion, user satisfaction and how well models respond to corrections, then scores each model by its net percentage improvement over an average competitor. Qwen 4 Max posted a preliminary 7.46% score across 14,727 sessions, the highest among Chinese entries.

Its visual work may be the more interesting part for regular users. The Code Arena web-development ranking compares websites built by AI models using head-to-head user votes and a points-based rating system. Qwen 4 Max debuted sixth globally at 1,750 points, up 74 from its predecessor, and placed eighth in categories for branding and reference-based design.

That puts it in the same neighborhood as the best American models at turning a request, a screenshot or a rough idea into a working interface that actually looks good.

Alibaba's demos go further, showing the model building game environments and translating factory layouts into 3D models, although those are company-selected examples rather than independent tests.

The visual capability is for understanding images and video and producing code or other text-based outputs. It is not the same as releasing a new image generator.

Qwen 4 Max costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million generated tokens through QwenCloud, a 25% reduction from the previous flagship's $2 and $6 rates. Reused input served from an automatic cache costs $0.075 per million tokens, which can make repetitive workflows substantially cheaper.

Alibaba says its internal testing across hundreds of professional specialties found that the model used 35% fewer tokens and reduced average task costs by roughly 60% compared with Qwen 3.8 Max. In other words, it should be cheaper to execute tasks on this model even against competitors with a similar price..

The bigger limitation for the community is that Qwen 4 Max is closed-weight. Developers can use it through an API or Alibaba's apps, but they cannot download its internal parameters, modify it or run it privately on their own hardware.

Qwen has become a foundation for the open-model ecosystem. An August report from Hugging Face counted 151,448 Qwen-based derivative models on its platform, about 4.7 times the number built specifically on Meta's Llama family. Those include community fine-tunes and optimized versions that power local assistants and specialized tools.

Alibaba opened the weights of Qwen 3.8 Max earlier this year, despite having kept some previous Max models proprietary. It also previewed elements of the Qwen 4 architecture with smaller models months before Monday's release.

The launch lands in a crowded Chinese race. Moonshot's Kimi K3 pushed enormous open-weight models toward Western performance, while DeepSeek has been competing hard on API prices.

Qwen 4 Max leads some Chinese rankings, but American labs still hold the top spots in Arena's overall agent and web-development tables. They are also considerably more expensive.

Alibaba says smaller Qwen 4 models will be released with open weights, giving developers a chance to build on this generation rather than simply rent its biggest model. It has not announced their sizes or release dates.

#4878. Custodia Bank loses Supreme Court bid for direct Fed payment access

The Supreme Court refused to hear Custodia Bank’s appeal, meaning a lower court ruling allowing the Fed to reject account applications will stand.

The United States Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear an appeal from crypto-focused bank Custodia, effectively ending the bank’s latest legal effort to gain direct access to the Federal Reserve’s payment system.

Custodia is a Wyoming-chartered bank founded by Caitlin Long. The bank has been trying for a Fed master account since 2020, which would allow it to process payments directly without relying on third-party financial institutions.

Now, the Supreme Court’s Monday decision means an earlier ruling allowing the Fed to reject applications from eligible banks will remain in effect.

The case highlights some of the challenges crypto-facing banks face in gaining direct access to the US payment system. Still, even if state-chartered banks qualify for master accounts, the Fed does not have to approve every application.

In a dissent issued in March, US Circuit Judge Timothy Tymkovich criticized the appeals court’s decision to give Federal Reserve banks discretion over master accounts.

“Without a master account, a bank cannot operate in the modern banking system,” Tymkovich wrote, arguing that the ruling effectively gives the Fed the power to override state banking decisions.

Custodia first sued the Federal Reserve in 2022 after waiting around two years for a decision on its master account application. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City ended up rejecting the request in January 2023, citing concerns about risks linked to the bank’s crypto-focused business model.

In October 2025, a federal appeals court ruled against Custodia, finding that Federal Reserve banks did not have to grant master accounts to every eligible institution.

Related: Crypto among sectors ‘debanked’ by 9 major banks: US regulator

Cointelegraph previously reported that the court declined to reconsider its decision in March. This led Custodia to take its case to the Supreme Court.

The bank’s appeal also received support from the Blockchain Association, which argued that the Fed’s ability to reject applications could weaken the authority of state banking regulators.

Senator Cynthia Lummis and former Senator Patrick Toomey also filed a brief with the Supreme Court in August, supporting Custodia’s appeal.

Today’s decision comes as other crypto-focused banks seek access to the Fed’s payment system. In March, Kraken Financial received approval for a restricted account from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City — the same regional bank that rejected Custodia’s application.

Notably, Kraken’s account was approved for an initial one-year period and allows it to send and receive payments through the Fed’s Fedwire system. However, the account has restrictions and does not offer all the services of a full master account.

Looking ahead, Custodia may still be able to apply for another master account or seek limited access to the Fed’s payment system under a separate proposal.

#4877. Solana Foundation Backs CoinGecko as Crypto Data Giant Eyes Trading

Solana Foundation Backs CoinGecko as Crypto Data Giant Eyes Trading

CoinGecko, one of crypto’s most widely used price-tracking sites, wants to do more than show users where markets are heading.

The crypto data platform said Tuesday that it has received backing from the Solana Foundation, the Switzerland-based nonprofit that supports the Solana network, to speed its expansion into market intelligence, new digital asset products and, potentially, trading.

The announcement came on the final day of Solana’s Breakpoint conference in London.

The Solana Foundation did not specify the size of the commitment, but a representative for the foundation told Decrypt it is taking a majority stake in CoinGecko. The terms were not disclosed.

CoinGecko said it will focus on three areas: expanding data coverage and analytics across blockchain ecosystems, exploring trading features that let users act onchain, and building simpler experiences for users worldwide.

“We’ve helped millions of people discover and understand this industry, but the opportunity ahead is much bigger,” said Bobby Ong, CoinGecko’s CEO and co-founder.

Vibhu Norby, chief product officer at the Solana Foundation, said the foundation believes the “next wave of adoption will come from making crypto dramatically easier to use.” (Disclosure: Decrypt’s parent company, Dastan, is building products on Solana, and Decrypt uses CoinGecko market data.)

Founded in 2014, CoinGecko says it provides data on more than 50 million crypto assets across more than 2,000 exchanges.

CoinGecko said it will keep serving users with the same commitment to “reliable, comprehensive market coverage and transparent methodologies.” Co-founder and President TM Lee said its commitment to accurate, reliable data “remains unchanged.”

The deal is one of several Solana announcements timed around Breakpoint. DTCC said last week that it plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana, with tokenized stocks, ETFs and Treasuries expected on the network in the second half of 2027.

At a Breakpoint panel, executives from DTCC and Barclays said tokenization’s biggest near-term payoff lies in putting idle collateral to work.

Editor's note: This article was updated after publication to include comment from the Solana Foundation.

It’s made from a blend of acetate (a semi-synthetic fiber derived from wood pulp—known for a silky feel and subtle sheen) and polyester, which gives this pant that drapey fit. The only downside is the care: it’s hand wash, line dry, which isn’t always the most convenient if you need to freshen up mid-trip.

If comfort is your top priority, the Skims Cotton Jersey Foldover Pant is the softest pair in the lineup. This is the kind of pant I put on for a flight and immediately feel better—like I’m wearing my favorite pajamas but still look pulled together enough to step off the plane without a full outfit change. It’s an ideal pant for long-haul days, early morning departures, or anytime you just want to feel cozy without fully leaning into sleepwear or baggy silhouettes.

It’s made from a jersey blend (mostly cotton with a touch of elastane), which is what gives it that ultra-soft, slightly stretchy feel. Cotton keeps things breathable and gentle against the skin, while elastane adds just enough give for when you’re sitting, walking, or curled up in a window seat. The foldover waistband is a standout feature—it lets you customize the rise depending on your preference, whether you want a more low-slung, relaxed fit or a bit more coverage. The fabric has that smooth, second-skin quality that moves with you, making it especially great for travel days when comfort is non-negotiable.

That said, it’s more versatile than you might expect. I’ll wear it with a simple tank and sneakers for an easy airport look, but it also works with a structured jacket to feel a bit more put-together. It also packs down to almost nothing, making it a great backup option in your carry-on. The one trade-off is that it does lean more casual—so while it’s perfect for the plane and low-key plans, it’s not quite as polished as some of the other options here.

Travel pants should follow that same philosophy: versatile enough to style casually with sneakers and a tee, but polished enough to pair with a blouse or blazer. Building multiple outfits around one reliable piece avoids overpacking and makes dressing while on vacation way easier.

#4875. Judge Acquits MIT Brothers in $25M Ethereum MEV Case, Ending Prosecution

Judge Acquits MIT Brothers in $25M Ethereum MEV Case, Ending Prosecution

A federal judge in Manhattan has acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno, the MIT-educated brothers accused of exploiting Ethereum's transaction ordering system to take $25 million from automated trading bots.

U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke granted the brothers' motion for a judgment of acquittal on Monday, clearing them of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to her ruling. The decision closes the criminal case without a second trial.

"The question before the Court is not whether the Peraire-Buenos' conduct was right or moral, or even whether it violated uncharged crimes," Clarke wrote. To convict on wire fraud, prosecutors had to show the brothers made a material misrepresentation, and none of the government's theories did so, she found. Ethereum, she noted, is a "trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use."

While the brothers' scheme "may have frustrated the spirit" of MEV-Boost, software that lets Ethereum validators outsource the ordering of transactions to specialized block builders, that was not enough to make out fraud, Clarke said. In a footnote, she added that the prosecution "raises serious due process concerns," though she declined to rule on that question.

Because the money laundering charge relied on the proceeds of the alleged wire fraud, it fell with the fraud counts.

The case stemmed from an April 2023 exploit targeting so-called sandwich bots, automated traders that profit from maximal extractable value (MEV) by placing their own trades on either side of other users' transactions.

According to the ruling, the brothers placed bait transactions designed to lure specific bots, then exploited a bug in a relay's code to see the bots' bundled trades before committing to a block. They then swapped the bait transactions for trades that sold the tokens instead, leaving the bots with about $25 million in losses in roughly 12 seconds. Authorities arrested the pair in May 2024, saying they spent months planning the attack and took steps to hide the proceeds.

At trial in Manhattan last year, an insider testified that the brothers had allegedly planned the attack, and the defense had earlier sought to block evidence of their Google searches. Clarke declared a mistrial in November 2025, after the jury deadlocked.

The case was closely watched in the crypto industry. Clarke's ruling described it as a "first of its kind" prosecution, a label the government itself used in its indictment.

#4874. Nvidia shares fall 4% as board reportedly rules out Huang return

The chipmaker’s board is reportedly focused on investigating Huang’s conduct, even as a petition calling for his reinstatement gathers more than 187,000 signatures.

Nvidia’s board is reportedly not considering reinstating co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, despite a growing campaign for his return and public support from US President Donald Trump, as the chipmaker’s shares fell 4.1% on Monday.

The decline came as Bitcoin and US equities faced pressure ahead of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings and following Anthropic’s IPO announcement, adding to nerves around the artificial intelligence sector.

A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that Nvidia’s board was not discussing Huang’s return and remained focused on investigating his conduct. ABC News separately confirmed with a source familiar with the matter that the board was not considering reinstating him as CEO.

Huang resigned last week following reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy, with chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. Nvidia’s shares have fallen 27% from a month ago.

The report comes despite growing support for his return. A public petition set up last week called “Stand with Jensen” has attracted more than 187,000 signatures, according to its organizers, who list Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its supporters.

US President Donald Trump also weighed in, saying Monday he would not mind seeing Jensen Huang return as chief executive officer of Nvidia.

“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told reporters as he departed the White House for a trip to China. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”

#4871. Nvidia Board Not Considering Jensen Huang's Return: Report

Nvidia Board Not Considering Jensen Huang's Return: Report

Nvidia's board is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, despite a growing campaign for his return led by some of the biggest names in tech and backed by President Donald Trump.

The board is focused on its investigation into Huang and is not in discussions to reinstate him, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday. The independent investigation, led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, is examining Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded. His departure followed his admission of an affair and reports that he had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at an Nvidia customer whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China, as well as with Nvidia employees. The week of revelations saw hundreds of billions of dollars wiped from Nvidia's market value.

The report cuts against a weekend of growing pressure for Huang's return. The Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed a comeback with allies, though Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, one of the investors urging the board to keep "all options" open, told CNBC that Huang had not discussed returning with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the speculation.

An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement had drawn 191,996 signatures by Monday. Its backers include Elon Musk, who said on Friday that he was signing it, as well as Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The site notes that signatories' affiliations are self-reported and unverified. Nvidia employees have also pushed internally for his return.

Trump said on Monday that he would welcome Huang back. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters, adding that national security had not been put at risk, as Decrypt reported. That puts him at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for its next CEO.

Others in tech have stopped short of backing a return. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was briefly ousted from his own company in 2023, said at a Semafor conference on Monday that Huang had "long been a hero of mine," but that he did not know enough to say whether Huang should come back.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% at $156.14 on Monday, and were down a further 0.5% at $155.67 in premarket trading early on Tuesday, according to Yahoo! Finance data.

Nvidia's board said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, the interim CEO, will lead the company's quarterly earnings call on Tuesday.

#4870. Hackers inject credit card, crypto-stealing malware into 178 major websites

Ledger and Coinpass were among the businesses whose websites served malware designed to steal visitors’ crypto and credit card details, according to security researchers.

Update (Nov. 17 at 4:43 am UTC): This article has been updated to include a statement from Salesforce and analysis of the stolen funds by Galaxy Digital’s Alex Thorn.

Update (Nov. 18 at 4:50 pm UTC): This article has been updated to include a statement from OANDA on behalf of Coinpass and TMS Brokers.

Major global brands including Ledger, Salesforce and BBC served cryptocurrency and credit card-stealing malware to website visitors on Monday, according to security researchers, the latest in a wave of wide-reaching cyberattacks.

Dubbed “Optimjack” by researcher Amirul Iman, the campaign delivered malicious code through website scripts, including those hosted by Optimizely, a website optimization platform. The malware can replace legitimate cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled alternatives when visitors copy addresses. It also captured credit card details entered into website forms, according to a separate analysis by cybersecurity firm StepSecurity.

The campaign affected website scripts belonging to 178 organizations, including hardware wallet Ledger, OANDA / Coinpass and trading platforms IG, Interactive Investor and TMS Brokers, according to Report URI’s investigation.

Other affected brands included IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, the BBC and CNN — websites that collectively attract millions of visitors a day.

A spokesperson for Optimizely confirmed to Cointelegraph on Monday that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

“We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix,” they said. “We have removed the injected code from affected projects. We have also ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts. Finally, we have blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare,” they said, adding that they’re continuing to investigate and have notified all affected customers.

BBC was among the first websites seen serving the Optimizely injection at 4:21 am UTC on Monday, according to Report URI CEO Scott Helme. By 9:52 pm UTC, only one of the 188 infected snippets still contained malicious code, with Ledger’s snippet cleaned at about 8:41 pm UTC.

Cointelegraph reached out to Ledger, Coinpass, and a number of other major businesses reported as impacted by the malicious injection.

An OANDA spokesperson, responding on behalf of Coinpass and TMS Brokers, told Cointelegraph on Tuesday that its security team had begun reviewing its environment following the Optimizely incident.

“Our internal systems and infrastructure were not breached, and we have seen no indication of any impact on client funds or account data. We are continuing to monitor the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for Salesforce told Cointelegraph it was investigating unauthorized modifications to Optimizely scripts used on certain Salesforce websites.

“As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

Optimizely lets businesses run experiments and custom code on their websites through JavaScript snippets. Attackers inserted malicious code into those customer projects, causing otherwise legitimate scripts to load the malware when visitors opened affected pages.

Once loaded, the malware could replace legitimate cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled alternatives, including addresses copied to a visitor’s clipboard. A user could then unknowingly paste the attacker’s address when making a transfer.

Related: PHP flaw draws millions of exploit attempts, Cloudflare CEO warns

The script also watched for credit card numbers, expiry dates and security codes entered into website forms and sent captured details to an attacker-controlled server. However, it could not read payment fields isolated inside third-party payment providers’ cross-origin frames, StepSecurity said.

Visitors using iPhones and iPads also faced an additional threat: the malicious script loaded code linked to the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits, according to Helme.

Researchers have yet to establish how attackers obtained access to modify the Optimizely projects.

Despite the widespread attack, crypto addresses identified as linked to the malware received only around $7,100 in cryptocurrency on Monday, according to blockchain records checked by Cointelegraph.

StepSecurity’s separate analysis put funds received or held across the wallets at roughly $6,600, noting that some addresses had activity predating the attack.

Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy Digital, estimated that victims have only sent around $2,300 in total to the addresses. In an analysis posted on X, Thorn said most of the Bitcoin receipts appeared to be the attacker’s own funds routed through an exchange back to their wallet, rather than proceeds from victims.

The campaign follows a string of recent threats to website security. In October, government agencies and other organizations took websites offline as a precaution over critical PHP vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to take control of servers. Polymarket also temporarily suspended trading on Oct. 29 after a third-party provider was compromised, amid reports of users’ accounts being drained.

I’ve tested more bras than I can count as a style writer. And over the years, I’ve learned that comfort is a nonnegotiable—if it digs, pinches, or rides up, it doesn’t deserve a space in my drawer. And if your usual size suddenly stops working? Totally normal. Bra fitter and undergarment educator Kimmay Caldwell says weight changes, hormone shifts, or your monthly cycle can impact your size. To make it trickier, some brands still use outdated sizing methods (like the “plus four” rule), while others go by your exact underbust. The most comfortable bras usually come down to the right blend of fabrics. Here’s what each one brings to the table:

Comfort is about more than just size—it’s also about ensuring the wire doesn’t create pressure points or cause discomfort throughout the day. Look for bras with flexible, padded, or cushioned underwires, which offer support without digging into your skin. The underwire should sit flat against your ribcage and follow the natural curve of your breasts. If it feels like it’s poking or shifting, it’s not the right fit. If you prefer a wire-free bra, opt for styles with flexible boning, molded cups, and wide, flexible bands to provide support.

The most accurate way to find your size is to get fitted in person. Once you have your size, your new bra should feel snug and secure. The band should be comfortably tight, but not dig into the skin. A good rule of thumb is that you should be able to fit two fingers between the band and your skin, but no more. The cups should also lie flat against your chest.

We wore them under different circumstances, including workouts, lounging, and long days at the office. But our main criterion for each bra was comfort. I also spoke with two bra experts and personally tested 20-plus bras over several years to lock down the ones I actually wear on repeat.
