#4868. Bunny Williams Never Set Out to Collect Birdhouses—Now a Whole Village of Them Stands in Her Connecticut Garden

Among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha. Each is raised high on its own post, finished on every side, painted and weathered like the structures of a settled town—and none has a door you could fit a hand through. It is a hamlet fashioned for birds, assembled building by building, the way real towns often grow: slowly, and without a master plan.

For many years as Williams and her husband, the antiques dealer John Rosselli, combed fields and fairs for Treillage, the much-loved shop they ran in New York City until 2015, the birdhouses kept finding her. They gathered on shelves in the hayloft of her barn. “When I had two, I didn’t know what to do with them,” she says. “Then all of a sudden there were 10.” She decided they had been in storage long enough.

A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.

An A-frame house embellished with gingerbread trim and decorative brackets

Williams, on a tree stump next to the pagoda. The notch in the base of the birdhouse indicates that it was probably designed to be mounted on a roof.

At that point, Williams and Robert Reimer, head gardener on her property, started the process of reclaiming a long-overlooked point of land. To create space and liberate a stand of existing apple trees, they removed invasive species, then planted oat grass, bird-friendly scrub plants, and fruit-bearing pawpaw trees. To create the neighborhood, she had uniform posts made—tall, “so that you look up at them,” each wrapped with a metal band to deter ambitious squirrels from climbing too high and disturbing the tenants she had in mind. Finally, up went the houses, now totaling 17.

The attraction had nothing to do with value or pedigree. “Most of these birdhouses are sort of folk art,” she says. “They were somebody having fun building an unusual structure.” Not Monticello in miniature, not a replica of someone’s own house, just unknown makers, each with “an eye and a kind of humor,” none of them trying to be perfect. The proof is in the details: the gingerbread scallops on one many-holed high-rise (“somebody had a great time with their little saw”), the thatched-roof cottage she prizes because she has never seen another like it, the weather vane crowning the would-be dacha.

A church with a brick chimney, an oversized cupola, and Gothic Revival design elements.

A rare combination house and feeder that evokes a neoclassical temple

Williams calls this one the general store.

A colonial revival house with a columned portico built by Larry Smith

“It has a kind of Russian dacha feeling,” says Williams.

What she didn’t have was history—the dealers who sold them seldom had any to pass along. The record, it turns out, is often recoverable. “The period from 1890 to 1930 is really the birdhouse’s golden age,” says Jacob Torkelson, an architectural historian and researcher at the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design, and among the very few scholars in the country studying these objects, whose makers and manufacturers he has painstakingly been identifying, where a name survives. Across those decades, government pattern books encouraged farmers to install birdhouses to reduce pesticide use (the birds would eat the insects), while mail-order companies offered them to homeowners as pure whimsy, not to mention a way of promoting biodiversity in their gardens. Shown photographs of Williams’s collection, Torkelson supplied some of what the dealers couldn’t. He traced one house down to the catalog page: the six-room Bungalow Martin House sold by the E.F. Hodgson Company, which listed the model from about 1917 until the firm closed in 1944. “Birdhouses are these wonderful mirrors to the human condition,” Torkelson says. “They tell us the values that we have as a society or as individuals, in our houses, in our gardens.”

A double porch house also built by Larry Smith

This pagoda-inspired birdhouse provides multiple roosting spots.

An unusual thatched-roof cottage prized by Williams, who has never seen another like it.

Williams isn’t finished collecting. Last May at Trade Secrets, the annual Litchfield Hills garden fair she cofounded in 2001 to raise funds for a local nonprofit domestic violence support agency, she stopped at the tent of Jim Sidon, whose company, Sparrow 10:29, crafts avian-size replicas of real buildings. Sidon, based outside Atlanta, came to the work after retiring from the printing industry. His first architectural birdhouse, built in 2017, was a replica of the 1792 Federal-style mansion in Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he and his wife had rented two rooms as newlyweds. It was Sidon who recognized, in three of Williams’s houses, the hand of his late friend Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for his metal roofs and charmingly rustic details. Williams has asked Sidon to build her something new, though she is still deciding exactly what. Unlike her anonymous makers, Sidon numbers and signs every house. “My hope is that years from now, someone’s searching that out,” he says, “and when they open it up, they’ll see my signature.”

A dovecote-inspired birdhouse offers multiple residences

A picturesque house topped with a prominent weather vane

Drawing the eye like miniature garden follies, the houses rise on poles amid a stand of apple trees from ground planted with oat grass and bird-friendly scrub plants.

In Falls Village, the upkeep routine is minimal: Every couple of years the houses come down, receive a coat of wood preservative, and go back up into the weather. Sidon’s constructions, with cedar exteriors and sealed against the elements, ask even less. His replica of the Newburyport house has stood in his own garden for nearly a decade untouched. “I just hose it off,” he says. None of this troubles Torkelson, a preservationist by training. “These houses were made to be ephemeral,” he says. “They weren’t made to last forever, and they should absolutely be used.”

As for the intended residents? Williams thinks the birds mostly prefer making their homes in the trees, where they carry on, she says, like a symphony orchestra: “I’ve always felt that one of the reasons they don’t live in these houses is the birds think it’s suburbia. But they like the atmosphere.” Come winter, when the woods go bare and the village shows through the branches, Sidon would bet the houses do get used, songbirds crowding in two and three at a time for warmth. Williams can’t say—she has never once climbed up to look. “If they are nesting,” she says, “I don’t want to bother them.”

#4867. Trezor customer data exposed in 3rd partner breach this year

Trezor warned an attacker has been able to access customer names, phone numbers and delivery addresses linked to 27,000 orders from one of its shipping providers.

Hardware wallet maker Trezor has disclosed its third partner data breach this year, warning that an attacker accessed personal information linked to approximately 27,000 orders held by shipping provider Skladon.

The exposed information includes customers’ names, phone numbers, delivery addresses, email addresses and purchase details for orders placed between Aug. 9 and Nov. 7.

Trezor said Monday that it believes the attacker exported the data. Its own systems were not compromised, and customers’ devices remain secure, the company said.

The disclosure follows an August breach at shipping provider ShipMonk that initially affected about 13,700 customers. Trezor later said another approximately 67,000 US customers were affected, including people whose records ShipMonk had assured it were deleted.

In September, a separate breach at marketing platform Brevo exposed 347,149 email addresses from Trezor’s newsletter list.

“Treat any unexpected call, text, email or letter about your order as suspicious, and be alert to potential risks to your physical security,” the company said on X. “Trezor will never cold-call you or ask for your wallet backup.”

The disclosure came as Trezor launched its anonymous pickup service in 18 European countries, allowing customers to order devices without giving out home addresses.

“For crypto holders, a leaked shipping record does more harm than most. It links a person, a home address and the fact that they own crypto,” it said.

#4866. Optimizely Hack Hijacked Ledger, BBC and 176 Other Sites to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses

Optimizely Hack Hijacked Ledger, BBC and 176 Other Sites to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses

An attacker hijacked Optimizely, a platform widely used by companies to run experiments on their websites, to serve malware that swapped visitors' crypto wallet addresses for their own, on sites including hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Optimizely said in a status update on Monday evening that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation product to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. The company said it had fixed the flaw, removed the injected code, secured affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code being delivered.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

— Optimizely (@Optimizely) November 17, 2026

Researchers at security firm Report URI, which sells tools to detect malicious website scripts, found the malicious code in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts they examined, belonging to 178 organizations, according to a blog post by founder Scott Helme. The affected sites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and HSBC, as well as crypto and trading firms such as Ledger, IG and OANDA.

Because the code was served from Optimizely's own trusted servers, affected websites loaded it without their own systems being breached.

The malware's main purpose was to steal crypto. The script scanned web pages for valid wallet addresses on networks including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana and TON, and replaced them with addresses controlled by the attacker, according to Report URI. It also swapped addresses copied to a user's clipboard, meaning anyone who copied an address while an affected page was open could have pasted the attacker's instead.

The attacker's wallets received about $7,150 in crypto, mostly in Bitcoin, Litecoin and USDT, according to Report URI's update on Tuesday. The attacker emptied the wallets early on Tuesday. One Tron address used to cash out had also been used in earlier operations in March and on November 3, allowing Report URI to link the attacker to other attacks, the firm said.

The script also skimmed card details typed into some sites' own payment forms, though not those entered into hosted payment fields such as Stripe's, and on iPhones and iPads it attempted to load exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword, which target older versions of iOS. Report URI said it could not see how many card numbers were stolen or how many devices were compromised.

The injected code first appeared early on November 16 UTC, and had been removed from all of the scripts Report URI could find by late that evening.

Optimizely spokesperson Victoria Johnson told Gizmodo that an unauthorized party had "exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow," and that the company had blocked access to the vulnerable path, deployed a fix and notified all affected customers. The company has not said how the attacker gained access to other customers' projects.

Helme said visitors to affected sites on November 16 should check any crypto transfers they made, update their iPhones and iPads, and watch their card statements. Website operators should review custom code in their Optimizely projects and rotate credentials, he added.

Our fave option on this list is from Beyond Yoga.

From Pilates to outdoor runs to heavy lifting sessions, I know exactly what separates a top you forget you’re wearing from one you can’t wait to peel off. This tank is meant to be worn over your favorite sports bra as an added layer of coverage. The tank is made with cotton, but it also has a bit of spandex woven throughout, which makes it stretchy and not too sturdy. This is essential during workouts, as you want your top to move with you instead of against you at the gym.

We noticed that the shirt can look a bit boxy if you go too oversized, so we recommend sizing down for a more flattering, snug fit.

Worried about the lighter colors looking sheer? Don’t be! All styles come with removable cups to cover your girls, which is also helpful because you can take them out when you wash the bra. One thing to keep in mind is that the straps aren’t adjustable, which can be a bit frustrating since it means you can’t customize the fit. I also wish it came in more colors.

This tank won the top spot in our Best Workout Tank Tops story for a few reasons: It's super flattering, never rides up, is compressive, supportive, and sweat-wicking.

We tested this ribbed tank across many different workouts—running, yoga, lifting, and HIIT—and we found that it never moves or rides up. Should your workout top be loose or tight? While it does come down to personal preference, there are pros and cons to each. For bigger busts or high-intensity activities, a built-in bra may not provide enough support, so you might need an extra sports bra underneath. #4864. The 9 Most Beautiful States in the US

The most beautiful states in the US prove just how shockingly diverse the country is: volcanic beaches, glacier-capped peaks, canyon-carved deserts, and misty rainforests define their landscapes. What people have built in those places is just as varied, from a royal palace in downtown Honolulu to Mary Colter’s stone watchtower on the rim of the Grand Canyon to the cedar-shingled studios of a modernist craft school on the coast of Maine. These nine states stand out on both counts, for the scenery that defines them and the architecture that holds its own against it. Keep in mind that no ranking can settle which state is most beautiful—they’re all worthy of a visit.

Hawaii is far from a monolithic state, with scenery changing from island to island. In Honolulu on Oahu, ʻIolani Palace, completed in 1882 for King Kalākaua, is the only royal palace on US soil—and it had electricity before the White House did.

Near Diamond Head, Doris Duke’s oceanfront estate, Shangri La, pairs 1930s modernism with architectural elements she brought from Morocco, Iran, Syria, and beyond. It’s now a museum of Islamic art, with tours departing from the Honolulu Museum of Art.

As for the natural landscape, Kauai, known as the Garden Isle, is home to the Nā Pali Coast, where green ridges drop sharply toward the Pacific. On Maui, Haleakalā’s broad volcanic summit often rises above a blanket of clouds. And on the Big Island, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park actively showcases the raw power of volcanoes—if you’re lucky, you might even catch an eruption.

Wyoming’s most famous photo moment might be the Teton Range rising abruptly above the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole, ideally with one of Mormon Row’s weathered homestead barns in the foreground. Nearby, the tiny log Chapel of the Transfiguration, built in 1925, was sited so that the picture window behind its altar frames the peaks where stained glass would normally go.

In Yellowstone National Park, it’s all about color: Grand Prismatic Spring’s vivid rings stand out among the forested landscape, while the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone exposes ochres and pinks in its steep walls. And steps from its namesake geyser, the Old Faithful Inn—designed by a 29-year-old Robert Reamer and opened in 1904—wraps a soaring lodgepole-pine lobby around a massive stone fireplace. It’s considered the largest log structure in the world.

Florida’s beaches are perhaps the state’s most scenic draw, but the architecture is just as distinctive. In 1979, Miami Beach’s Art Deco District, roughly a square mile of South Beach, became the nation’s first urban 20th-century historic district on the National Register, with more than 800 buildings listed. Across Biscayne Bay, industrialist James Deering’s Vizcaya, a villa completed in 1916, faces the water with formal gardens by Diego Suarez. Addison Mizner gave Palm Beach its Mediterranean Revival look; his Via Mizner, a winding pedestrian lane off Worth Avenue built in 1923, survives today.

St. Augustine, founded by the Spanish in 1565, pairs the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos with Henry Flagler’s Hotel Ponce de Leon, a Spanish Renaissance–style palace from 1888 that’s now Flagler College. Architecture buffs should detour to Lakeland, where Frank Lloyd Wright’s campus for Florida Southern College is the largest single-site collection of his architecture in the world. And on the Gulf Coast, Sarasota’s midcentury modernists adapted the International Style to the subtropics, most famously in Paul Rudolph’s 1953 Umbrella House.

On Maine’s coast, Acadia National Park packs a surprising amount of scenery into a small area: granite headlands, spruce forest, offshore islands, and views of the Atlantic. Look closely, and you'll notice the park’s impressive stonework, too. John D. Rockefeller Jr. financed its network of carriage roads, built between 1913 and 1940, along with 16 of the 17 stone-faced bridges that carry them over streams and gorges—no two are alike.

Don’t forget the coastal villages, from ever-popular Bar Harbor and its shingle-style and Queen Anne houses to Stonington, a working fishing town on Deer Isle. Elsewhere on Deer Isle, Edward Larrabee Barnes’s 1961 campus for the Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, an underrated masterpiece of American modernism, steps down a granite slope toward Jericho Bay, its cedar-shingled cabins and studios linked by boardwalks.

California has a little of everything, from the architectural hubs of Los Angeles and San Francisco to breathtaking natural settings. In Yosemite, El Capitan and Half Dome are jaw-dropping from the valley floor, but even more so from the top for those daring enough to make the climb. Back down in the valley, the Ahwahnee hotel, which opened in 1927, appears to be built of granite and redwood—but the “wood” is actually fireproof concrete, poured into molds and stained to look like timber. In the desert, Palm Springs is a showcase of midcentury modernism, with Richard Neutra’s 1946 Kaufmann House as its best-known example.

But the California coast is undeniably the state’s most famous landscape, and the 656 miles of Highway 1 deliver architecture along with the views. Above San Simeon, Hearst Castle, which Julia Morgan designed for William Randolph Hearst over nearly three decades, crowns a hilltop overlooking the Pacific. Continue north past the bluffs of Big Sur and storybook Carmel-by-the-Sea to the Sonoma Coast, where the redwood-clad buildings of the Sea Ranch, a planned community begun in the mid-1960s, are tucked into hedgerows to leave the meadows and bluffs open.

New York State’s famous architecture isn’t limited to the Manhattan skyline—though the city certainly pulls its weight on the architecture front. In the Adirondacks, wooded mountains surround lakes such as Lake Placid and the three Saranac Lakes. The “great camps” that wealthy families began building along their shores in the Gilded Age turned the log cabin into high style. You can still stay in one: The Point, on Upper Saranac Lake, was built in the early 1930s as Camp Wonundra for William Avery Rockefeller II and is now an 11-room Relais & Châteaux hotel, the first in North America.

In the Hudson Valley, painter Frederic Church’s hilltop villa, Olana, features a design style he called “Persian, adapted to the Occident.” The Finger Lakes offer a gentler landscape of long, narrow lakes bordered by vineyards and small towns, plus the gorge at Watkins Glen State Park, where a stone path meanders past tumbling cascades and swirling pools. And in Buffalo, you’ll find Frank Lloyd Wright’s Darwin D. Martin House, one of his finest Prairie-style designs.

The Grand Canyon is a tough act to follow, but on its South Rim, architect Mary Colter spent decades designing buildings meant to hold their own beside it. Her Hopi House, which opened in 1905, is a multistory stone building shaped like a Hopi pueblo; her Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, is a 70-foot stone tower modeled on Ancestral Puebloan structures, with a Snake Legend mural inside by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie.

Sedona’s red-rock buttes are spectacular on their own, but the Chapel of the Holy Cross, a modernist concrete chapel built directly into a pair of sandstone buttes and completed in 1956, gives them a focal point. North of Phoenix, Paolo Soleri’s Arcosanti, an experimental desert town of concrete domes and arches begun in 1970, is still a work in progress. And in Scottsdale, in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains, Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West—his winter home and studio from 1937 until his death in 1959—is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Texas’s landscapes range from the Chihuahuan Desert to the Gulf Coast to the bayous of Caddo Lake. In Big Bend National Park, the Chisos Mountains rise above dry plains, and the Rio Grande cuts through the narrow walls of Santa Elena Canyon. In Marfa, minimalist artist Donald Judd turned a former army post into the Chinati Foundation, a museum built around permanent, large-scale installations, including his 100 mill-aluminum boxes lined up inside two converted artillery sheds.

In Fort Worth, Louis Kahn’s Kimbell Art Museum, completed in 1972, draws architects from around the world to see natural light wash down its concrete cycloid vaults; Tadao Ando’s Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth sits just across the street. Central Texas has rolling hills, and in spring, bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush color the roadsides around Fredericksburg, a town with German heritage.

Mount Rainier is perhaps Washington’s most familiar landmark, its glaciers and snowfields visible above forests and summer wildflower meadows. The North Cascades offer even more peaks, with jagged ridges rising above turquoise Diablo Lake, while the trails in Olympic National Park lead through mossy rainforest and out to driftwood-strewn beaches.

Seattle holds its own against all that scenery. Downtown, the Central Library—designed by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA with local firm LMN and opened in 2004—wraps its stacked floors in a faceted net of glass and steel, while the Space Needle, built for the 1962 World’s Fair, remains the skyline’s signature. Outside Seattle, Port Townsend’s Victorian storefronts overlook the water, and in the Walla Walla Valley, vineyard rows and wheat fields spread across rolling hills, with the Blue Mountains rising beyond them.

#4863. 'The Biggest Opportunity in Crypto Is Already Underway': Solana Bets Big on AI Agents

'The Biggest Opportunity in Crypto Is Already Underway': Solana Bets Big on AI Agents

AI agents are becoming the internet's main users, and the Solana Foundation wants its blockchain to be how they pay for things.

"The biggest opportunity in crypto is already underway," Rishin Sharma, who leads AI at the Solana Foundation, said at the Breakpoint conference in London.

Sharma used his presentation to showcase Solana.ai, a new homepage for the network's AI ecosystem, which the foundation launched last week. More than 120 teams are now building AI products on Solana across payments, trading and infrastructure, he said.

Bots and other automated software accounted for more than 53% of global web traffic in 2025, up from 51% the year before, according to cybersecurity firm Imperva's latest Bad Bot Report, which Sharma cited. Agents have also come to dominate AI usage: API keys classified as agentic accounted for 76% of the tokens processed through model marketplace OpenRouter in October 2026, up from 8% a year earlier, according to the company's monthly data recap.

At the same time, AI is getting much cheaper. Sharma's slides showed the price of a million tokens falling from $37.50 for GPT-4 to $0.14 for GPT-5 nano, a 270-fold drop, while monthly token use has risen around 330-fold.

"Which model is smarter matters a little bit less, and what matters more is what the model can actually do," Sharma said. "What are the tools it's using? What are the data it's able to access? And what money can it functionally use?"

Payments are where that shift is showing up first, Sharma said. The x402 standard, which lets AI agents pay for online services, has processed more than 400 million payments and $100 million in volume, up from zero a year ago, he said. Solana-based BlockRun, which he described as the largest x402 server, has handled more than 60 million transactions in the past two months.

The foundation has also launched payment channels that it says can handle 1 million payments per second, a private AI service offering attested private inference on Solana, and Pay.sh, a server integrating more than 100 APIs that agents can pay for, Sharma said. He added that the foundation is working with companies including Google, Alibaba and ByteDance to let them charge for their AI models through agent payments.

Next, the foundation plans to publish benchmarks for how well AI models perform financial tasks, and to launch an on-ramp that lets users convert cash to stablecoins and hand them to their AI assistants, he said.

Macro investor and Real Vision founder Raoul Pal, speaking earlier at the conference, argued that agents are not yet real economic actors. "They're like kids," he said. "These are young kids who spend nothing on a few sweets and stuff." But as stocks and other assets move onchain, he said, agents will start using blockchains to trade and settle, and "the value accrues to the underlying layer one."

Solana has been building toward this for months. The foundation teamed up with Google Cloud on a stablecoin payments service for AI agents in May, while the x402 Foundation, backed by Coinbase and the Linux Foundation, is developing the payments standard. Franklin Templeton has described agentic AI as a killer use case for crypto.

The former Robinhood engineer used confidential information about upcoming Robinhood token listings to trade on Hyperliquid.

Former Robinhood software engineer Huaisong “Jerry” Xiang has pleaded guilty to wire fraud after using confidential information about upcoming crypto listings on the platform to trade perpetual futures on the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, earning $125,523 in illicit profits.

On Monday, the US Department of Justice said that Xiang entered the plea before US District Judge Colleen McMahon and agreed to forfeit $125,523. Xiang faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison and is scheduled to be sentenced on Feb. 25, 2027.

Prosecutors said the software engineer had access to nonpublic information about which tokens Robinhood Crypto planned to list and when. Between 2025 and 2026, he repeatedly bought perpetual futures tied to those tokens before the announcements were made public.

The DOJ’s Monday announcement did not provide an update on Chai’s case.

In May, crypto analytics firm Kaiko flagged suspicious Hyperliquid trading ahead of Robinhood’s Jan. 15 listing of Lighter (LIT). One of the wallets identified in its investigation matches an address that prosecutors later linked to Chai, who allegedly used it to trade LIT perpetuals ahead of the listing.

#4860. Goldman Sachs reports $1.22B in Ether ETFs as ETHA share count jumps

Goldman Sachs increased its Ether ETF shares in Q3, bringing its reported holdings to $1.22 billion, while reshuffling its Bitcoin ETF positions.

Banking giant Goldman Sachs reported $1.22 billion in Ether exchange-traded fund (ETF) holdings at the end of September, up from $211.6 million three months earlier, as it increased positions across several funds throughout the third quarter.

The bank increased its holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA) by 352% to 29.96 million shares, worth $602.9 million, according to its Q3 Form 13F filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

The company also shifted its Bitcoin ETF holdings, reducing its stake in BlackRock’s Bitcoin (BTC) fund while increasing its position in Fidelity’s competing ETF.

The increase coincided with a strong quarter for Ether (ETH), which surged nearly 71% in Q3, according to CoinGlass. US spot Ether ETFs attracted more than $3 billion in net inflows, their strongest quarter of 2026, according to SoSoValue.

BlackRock’s ETHA was not the only Ether ETF in which Goldman Sachs increased its holdings during Q3.

The bank also increased its holdings in Grayscale’s Ethereum Staking Mini ETF (ETH) by 180% to 5.68 million shares, lifting the position’s reported value to $144.9 million from $30.5 million in Q2.

Its holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Staked Ethereum ETF (ETHB) rose 62% to 8.18 million shares, worth $281 million, up from $102.3 million in the previous quarter.

Goldman also reported four additional Ether ETF positions worth a combined $195.4 million, led by $169.6 million in Fidelity’s Ethereum Fund (FETH).

Including the new positions, Goldman’s reported Ether ETF holdings reached approximately $1.22 billion at the end of Q3, up from $211.6 million in Q2.

Goldman reduced its IBIT holdings by about 792,000 shares to 16.44 million, although the position’s reported value increased 36% to $778.3 million as IBIT’s price surged 42% over the quarter.

Meanwhile, its FBTC holdings surged more than 50-fold, from 105,840 shares to 5.48 million, bringing their reported value to $397.9 million from just $5.4 million.

Camran Khosravi, research analyst at global asset manager Bitwise, told Cointelegraph that market makers such as Jane Street can shift between Bitcoin ETFs to meet client demand and hedge options positions without necessarily changing their overall Bitcoin exposure.

Related: Jane Street boosts Fidelity Bitcoin ETF holdings nearly 8x, trims IBIT

“13F filings can make routine market-making look like a big bet on one fund,” Khosravi said, noting that the disclosures omit short positions and other instruments that may offset reported holdings.

While Goldman trimmed its IBIT shares, Wells Fargo more than doubled its holdings in the BlackRock Bitcoin ETF. The bank’s Q3 filing showed its IBIT position rising 103% to 49.58 million shares, worth around $2.35 billion, while its ETHA holdings increased 125% to 22 million shares.

#4859. Morning Minute: The CFTC Officially Greenlights Perps in the US, Starting with Backpack

Morning Minute: The CFTC Officially Greenlights Perps in the US, Starting with Backpack

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals

For years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch. On Monday, that officially changed.

Chairman Michael Selig approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to run regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that execute and settle on blockchain rails. Selig called it “an important milestone in the evolution of American financial markets.”

Backpack got both pieces at once, a Designated Contract Market designation to run the exchange and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration to clear its own trades. It plans to offer Americans round-the-clock leveraged crypto perps on a single global order book, accepting both fiat and crypto as collateral with cross-margin across positions. tZERO received its exchange approval a week earlier, after already holding clearing registration, and is building it into a derivatives vertical inside its infrastructure business.

Backpack US president Mark Wetjen, himself a former CFTC commissioner, framed it as “moving price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.” CEO Armani Ferrante said the firm enters markets “fully regulated from day one.” Backpack already runs licensed platforms in Europe, Asia and the UAE.

The CFTC has certainly been busy this month. They cleared single-stock perpetual futures on November 3. It issued guidance on November 5 telling federally regulated exchanges they generally cannot restrict access by state. Now it has approved blockchain-native exchanges and clearinghouses.

Selig is building an onshore home for every product the offshore venues were built to serve, and he is doing it through staff action rather than legislation, with one sitting commissioner and nomination hearings for two more this week.

Hyperliquid is the obvious candidate and also the one that has publicly said it doesn’t want this. Jeff Yan spent his Bloomberg interview this month arguing Hyperliquid is infrastructure rather than an exchange, and that regulators should oversee the firms deploying markets on top rather than the chain underneath. His US route is HIP-3 partners taking on the compliance burden, with ICE investing in Trade.xyz and Kraken’s parent reportedly in talks. Backpack getting a DCM and a DCO makes that argument harder, because it demonstrates a crypto-native venue can simply register.

Then there’s Lighter. It has run Robinhood Wallet’s perps since July on a dedicated instance with a 50/50 revenue split, which is the partner model rather than the registration model. The registered model opens up with a CFTC license, and many think Lighter could very well be next.

One thing’s certain—the CFTC is serious about bringing perps onshore. From Selig himself, “I look forward to building on that milestone.” And we will find out soon enough who’s next…

#4858. US judge clears brothers in $25M Ethereum MEV case after mistrial

Judge Jessica Clarke said the transactions did not involve false promises, but the ruling did not determine whether the brothers’ conduct was ethical or violated other laws.

A US federal judge acquitted two brothers accused of extracting $25 million from Ethereum trading bots, ruling that prosecutors failed to prove they made material misrepresentations during the alleged exploit.

In a Monday ruling, Judge Jessica Clarke acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno on wire fraud and related charges. Prosecutors alleged that the MIT-educated brothers exploited a flaw in maximal extractable value (MEV)-boost software in April 2023 to lure sandwich-trading bots into transactions they then disrupted, securing $25 million in about 12 seconds.

The judge said the transactions did not amount to false promises or constitute criminal fraud, and that the case was not about whether the brothers’ actions were ethical or potentially violated other laws.

Their first trial ended in a mistrial when jurors failed to reach a verdict in November 2025.

Coin Center executive director Peter Van Valkenburgh called the acquittal “excellent news,” saying prosecutors’ honest validator theory risked allowing the government to impose its own standards of conduct on Ethereum validators through wire fraud laws.

“Anyone participating in an open network would have to wonder whether prosecutors might later declare their behavior ‘dishonest’ and haul them into court,” Valkenburgh said.

The ruling also cited a 2025 decision involving Mango Markets trader Avraham Eisenberg, where a judge found insufficient evidence of false representations.

#4857. Standard Life Chair Wants Tokenized Gilts to Open UK Government Bonds to Retail Savers

Standard Life Chair Wants Tokenized Gilts to Open UK Government Bonds to Retail Savers

Tokenization could help ordinary British savers buy government bonds more easily, and should not become a tool only for big financial institutions, according to Sir Nicholas Lyons, chairman of Standard Life.

"Why should it be so unnecessarily complicated for retail investors to buy gilts that fund the nation's needs?" Lyons said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London.

Lyons, a former Lord Mayor of the City of London whose company has about £480 billion ($633 billion) in assets under administration, said Britain should use tokenization to bring more households into investing. About £850 billion ($1.1 trillion) of household wealth remains in cash, often losing value to inflation, he said.

Tokenization could cut administrative costs, make transfers simpler and let savers invest in small amounts in products that would otherwise be uneconomic, Lyons said. More retail ownership of gilts would make the UK less reliant on foreign buyers and could help erode the risk premium the country has paid on its debt since the September 2022 mini-budget, he added.

The remarks come as the UK prepares to issue its first digitally native government bond, known as DIGIT. Earlier this month, the Treasury confirmed roles for six banks supporting the pilot, with issuance expected in the first quarter of 2027, Lyons said.

"Government bonds sit at the heart of our financial system," he said, noting that they underpin liquidity, provide collateral and set reference rates for other assets. Showing that tokenized gilts can be issued, settled and used as collateral efficiently would lay "an important foundation for much broader digital capital markets," he said.

Lyons credited the Financial Conduct Authority, the Bank of England and the Treasury for progress so far, including the Digital Securities Sandbox and work to let tokenized securities be used as collateral.

The Bank of England has also turned its attention to stablecoins: an executive has said it is treating them as a new form of money, it eased its planned stablecoin rules in June, and it has since been handed a legal duty to foster stablecoin innovation. Lyons cited a July report by Chris Woolard, the government's wholesale digital markets champion, which estimated that faster adoption of digital markets could add as much as £33 billion ($43.5 billion) a year to UK economic output by 2035.

But the competition is moving fast, he warned, pointing to the SEC's innovation exemption for tokenized stock trading in the U.S., and initiatives in Europe, Singapore, Hong Kong, Switzerland and the Middle East.

Lyons set out four priorities: making the digital gilt pilot a success, accelerating tokenized collateral and repo markets, promoting interoperability to avoid "a collection of competing digital platforms that recreate the fragmentation of the existing system," and ensuring retail investors share in the benefits.

He also acknowledged the risks, citing concerns raised by the Financial Times' Gillian Tett that AI-accelerated cyber threats and faster-moving money could fuel a run on deposits. "Tokenization does not automatically make an investment safer, more liquid, or more stable, or suitable for retail investors," he said. "Fractional ownership of a risky asset remains ownership of a risky asset."

"We're not pursuing tokenization for the sake of technological leadership," Lyons said. "We're pursuing better capital markets, more productive investment, greater economic prosperity, and wider participation in the creation of wealth and jobs."

#4856. Google says hackers use AI agents to find and exploit software flaws

Google says attackers are using AI agents to find and exploit software flaws automatically, reducing the time organizations have to apply patches.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it had, for the first time, identified attackers using AI large language model (LLM) frameworks to automate software vulnerability discovery and exploitation without step-by-step human direction.

In a report published Monday, the researchers described a tool found on an exposed staging server that compared software versions, identified potential flaws, and generated and executed exploit code.

“In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time,” the researchers said.

GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, set up to conduct continuous differential analysis comparing code before and after patch announcements on popular web applications. The model would autonomously discover and exploit software vulnerabilities.

Google warned that these automated workflows give organizations less time to apply security patches before attackers develop ways to exploit vulnerable systems.

In its September report, GTIG said it had “not yet observed threat actors deploying fully autonomous pipelines against targets in the wild.”

Evolution of threat actors using LLMs for exploits. Source: Google

Attackers are leveraging AI agent frameworks to automate patch reverse engineering via differential analysis and weaponizing N-day vulnerabilities, publicly known security flaws.

The report warned that LLMs are enabling attackers to scale “exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.”

Vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August, according to Google. The number of zero-day vulnerabilities exploited averaged eight per month in 2025 and 11 per month from January through August 2026, reaching 22 in August.

Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026. Source: Google

These automated workflows also accelerate attackers’ ability to move from initial access to gaining domain administrator access. The report cited an August 2026 PaperCut campaign in which attackers achieved that level of control within minutes, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise.

Related: PHP flaw shows AI ‘vulnerability apocalypse’ is on schedule: Immunefi CEO

Cloudflare also reported attempts to exploit the PHP flaws against its customers in October. GTIG said that the two PHP vulnerabilities involved in the exploitation attempts were discovered using LLM analysis, as technical information published before the Oct. 21 patch enabled researchers and attackers to study vulnerabilities and attempt exploits, according to the report.

AI company Anthropic also warned that AI-assisted attacks have evolved into multi-agent operations automating most of the cyberattack cycle from discovery to exploitation and data theft, in a September report.

Anthropic described threat actors running “multi-victim campaigns using agentic AI that would previously have required teams of operators.”

#4855. Healthy on the Outside: The Silent Risk Dr. Nancy Snyderman Never Saw Coming

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, spent decades helping millions of Americans understand their health. But when it came to her own health, it was a nudge from a friend that finally pushed her to get the care she really needed.

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, began her career caring for one patient at a time. After medical school, Nancy became a board-certified surgeon, working at academic medical centers, and she kept running into the same gap: the distance between what doctors knew and what patients actually understood about their own health. Television, she realized, could help close it. “A big part of being a doctor, for me, was putting humanity back into medicine,” she says. So she traded caring for one patient at a time for caring for all Americans.

For nearly three decades, Americans welcomed Nancy into their homes through their televisions. As a chief medical correspondent, she covered wide ranging medical topics and traveled the world extensively, reporting from many of the world’s most-troubled areas. Every day, she expertly translated complex medical news into easily digestible—and actionable—information for people across America.

“I spent my whole career being the person who talked about health to help others,” she says. “I never thought I’d be the one in need of help.”

Nancy has always been active. Even now, she hikes, travels and keeps up with her young grandchildren. But being active and feeling good doesn’t always mean you’re healthy. No one knows this better than Nancy, who had no symptoms of heart disease before her diagnosis. It started when she was still a national medical correspondent, working on a story on CT angiograms and a then-new test that provided a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score. As part of her report, Nancy had the scan done herself and her score came back at 100. “I thought, ‘Oh my gosh, this is great, I aced this test’,” she says—only to learn that acing it means a score of zero.

What is a CAC Scan?A coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan is an imaging test that measures the amount of calcified plaque built up in the heart's arteries.1 It can help doctors and patients understand cardiovascular risk—even before symptoms appear.1

At the same time, she was struggling to keep her LDL-C, or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called “bad” cholesterol, in check. High LDL-C is one of the leading risk factors for a heart attack or stroke, but also one of the most modifiable.2 To lower her LDL-C, Nancy had been taking statins—which are a commonly prescribed class of LDL-C lowering medication—for decades. “I knew what to do, and I thought I was doing the right things,” she says. “But I was never able to really get my bad cholesterol to my doctor-recommended level.”

What finally changed everything was a conversation. After reconnecting with an old friend, who also happens to be a cardiac nurse, Nancy mentioned her CAC score and stubborn LDL-C. Her friend insisted that Nancy see a new cardiologist. After some additional testing, the results were nothing Nancy ever expected to hear: severe coronary artery disease, with significant blockages in the arteries feeding her heart.

What is LDL-C?LDL-C stands for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol—often called “bad” cholesterol. When too much of it builds up in the blood, it can settle into artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.2

“My diagnosis was a huge wake-up call,” she says. “I thought I was doing the right things, but even I, as a physician, needed an advocate.” She’s quick to point out why that mattered: “A lot of the risks women face with heart disease can be managed,” she adds, “but only if we understand them and speak up for ourselves.”

Nancy’s experience is far more common than many women realize. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States3—yet only about half (56%) of women recognize it as their number one threat.3 “One of the most dangerous things about heart disease is how quietly it can develop,” says Sirisha Vadali, MD, a board-certified cardiologist in Scottsdale, Arizona. “It can progress silently, even when you feel completely healthy,4 and women in particular may not have the obvious warning signs we’ve all been taught to watch for.”

So much of that hidden risk traces back to a single number: LDL-C. When there’s too much of this “bad” cholesterol circulating, it doesn’t just sit in the blood. It works its way into the artery walls and builds up as a sticky plaque, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.5,6 “It isn’t only how high your LDL-C is today,” Dr. Vadali says. “It’s how high it has been, and for how long. The longer it’s too high, the more cardiovascular risk accumulates.”⁵

For Nancy, the lesson was humbling: expertise is not immunity. “You can be the most informed person in the room and still miss a health warning in yourself,” she says. It sometimes takes a push from a loved one to take the necessary action.

After her diagnosis, Nancy did exactly what she had spent years urging her viewers to do: she partnered with her cardiologist and built a plan. Together, they assessed her individual risk factors and set a clear target for her LDL-C to help lower her cardiovascular risk.

Getting there was more challenging than Nancy realized. “Despite standard treatment, diet, and exercise, my LDL-C was still too high, and we needed to lower it to my doctor-recommended LDL-C goal,” she says.

That gap—between lower and a guideline-recommended target—is one Dr. Vadali sees constantly. “When it comes to LDL-C, lower is better, but ‘lower’ isn’t the same as reaching the guideline-recommended goal for your unique risk factors,” she says.

What are the Guideline-Recommended Goals?The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends specific LDL-C goals based on individual risk. For example, below 70 mg/dL for people with diabetes and multiple cardiovascular risk factors, and below 55 mg/dL for those with cardiovascular disease at very high risk.7,*

“Knowing your LDL-C number—and talking with your doctor about what’s right for you—is one of the first steps toward understanding your risk level,” Dr. Vadali adds.

She’s also quick to retire a persistent myth. “For a lot of people, especially those already at increased cardiovascular risk, diet and exercise alone may not be enough to get LDL-C to the guideline-recommended goal,” Dr. Vadali says. “That’s not a personal failing. It’s biology. Sometimes the body needs additional help, and that’s worth a conversation with your doctor.”

For Nancy, that additional help became part of her plan. Working with her cardiologist, she started treatment with REPATHA® (evolocumab) to help lower her LDL-C and reduce her risk of a major cardiovascular event.

Repatha® is an injectable prescription medicine used:

Please see additional Important Safety Information below and full Prescribing Information.

These days, treatment is a welcome part of Nancy’s routine. “Every two weeks, I give myself an injection and have built a small ritual around it as part of my treatment plan to help keep my LDL-C at the goal my doctor recommended,” she says. “I can take it in the comfort of my own home or on the go† which is a treatment that can fit into my routine.”

Nancy is careful to say her path is her own. “I’m sharing my experience as a patient, but everyone’s situation is different,” she says. “What mattered was working with my doctor to figure out what was right for me. That’s what I want for every woman reading this to consider.”

Dr. Vadali says REPATHA is a treatment she has consistently recommended for appropriate patients. “I prescribe REPATHA because we know it starts working quickly,” she says. “For high-risk patients, keeping LDL-C lower will help reduce their risk of a life-altering event like a heart attack or stroke.”

If one thread runs through Nancy’s story, it’s the one so many women will recognize: the tendency to take care of everyone else first. “Women wear a lot of hats, and most of them involve caring for other people,” she says. “We don’t always stop to care for ourselves.”

That’s the habit she’s determined to break—in herself, and in the women who’ve heard important health messages from her for years. Her message today isn’t fear; it’s agency. “I want women to proactively understand their cardiovascular risk before something forces them to,” she says. “Ask the question: What’s my risk, and what can I do about it?”

Nancy’s ask is simple: Talk to your healthcare provider about your LDL-C and your personal cardiovascular risk factors. Get your LDL-C tested, know your doctor-recommended LDL-C goal and—if needed—make a plan with your doctor to help you reach it.

“This is the health story I never expected to tell,” Nancy says. “But if telling it means one more woman picks up the phone and calls her doctor, then it’s the most important one I’ve ever shared.”

#4854. Bitcoin realized loss metric beats June high as open interest eyes 2-year low

Bitcoin short-term holders’ onchain spending notched the largest proportion of realized losses since February after BTC/USD dropped to $62,000.

Bitcoin investors are showing increasing signs of panic as newer buyers’ onchain losses hit their highest since February.

Data from onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant reveals new nine-month lows in the spent output profit ratio (SOPR) of Bitcoin’s short-term holders (STH).

SOPR measures the ratio of BTC moving onchain at a higher or lower price relative to the last time it was used in a UTXO. The metric can be broken down by investor cohort, only accounting for coins owned by older or newer hodlers. The latter cohort traditionally consists of speculative entities who are more sensitive to BTC price volatility. An STH entity is a wallet holding a given unit of BTC for up to 155 days without selling.

On Nov. 16, STH-SOPR recorded a reading of 0.955, its lowest since Feb. 7. Readings below 1 reflect STH coins moving onchain on aggregate at a lower price compared to their previous transaction.

Noticeable deviations below 1 on STH-SOPR imply increased loss-making selling activity by the STH cohort. While BTC/USD briefly dipped to $62,000 this week, the latest reading is notably lower than in late June, when investors reacted to price hitting 20-month lows of $58,534 and STH-SOPR reached 0.985.

In its latest analysis released on Monday, Bitfinex Alpha, the research arm of crypto exchange Bitfinex, noted that in both June and July, swing lows on STH-SOPR corresponded to the “days of heaviest loss-taking” among speculators.

“Net realised losses across all holders reached about 76,500 BTC on 15 November, the largest since 1 July, a significant increase from about 18,700 BTC on 10 November,” it reported.

Bitcoin STH profitability comparison. Source: Bitfinex

Bitfinex added that unrealized losses reveal the pain levels of the broader Bitcoin investor base, with the share of the BTC supply held at loss reaching 48.5% on Nov. 14 — the same as on July 1, when BTC/USD set a new multiyear floor of $57,800.

“Holders are therefore under as much pressure as they were at that low, with price about 11 percent higher,” it wrote.

Speculative Bitcoin trading activity overall has witnessed a marked drop in recent weeks.

Related: BTC price tags 18-week low into Nvidia earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week

Open interest, the total number of active derivative positions, dropped to $20.498 billion on Tuesday, a level not seen since late 2024, as measured by CryptoQuant.

In commentary on Monday, CryptoQuant contributor Baykuş flagged a conspicuous drop in OI on Binance as BTC/USD fell from $74,000 to $64,000.

“Open interest on coin-margined BTC-USD contracts fell from $1.55B to $1.1B, and since these contracts are USD-denominated, this reflects real position closures,” they wrote in a blog post.

#4853. Former Robinhood Engineer Pleads Guilty to Crypto Insider Trading Scheme

Former Robinhood Engineer Pleads Guilty to Crypto Insider Trading Scheme

Former Robinhood software engineer Huaisong “Jerry” Xiang pleaded guilty Monday to wire fraud for using confidential plans for upcoming cryptocurrency listings to trade on Hyperliquid. The 30-year-old agreed to forfeit $125,523 in profits from the scheme, according to the Justice Department.

Xiang entered his plea before U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon on November 16, two months after prosecutors accused him and another Robinhood engineer of trading ahead of the brokerage's token announcements. He pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud; the DOJ announcement did not report a guilty plea to the commodities-fraud charge initially brought against him.

As a software engineer working on new listings for Robinhood Crypto, Xiang had access to a private Slack channel reserved for employees classified as “Coin Aware Individuals.” It contained information about which tokens were coming to the platform and when, according to the FBI complaint filed in September.

Robinhood's internal policy prohibited that group from trading around upcoming listings on any platform, not just Robinhood. The restriction began before a listing was announced and continued for 24 hours after it became public. A November 2024 email warned Xiang to “refrain from abusing access to or knowledge of this information,” the complaint says.

Investigators described one trade involving POPCAT, a Solana-based meme coin. After receiving internal messages about a planned March 13, 2025 listing, Xiang moved approximately 18 Ethereum, then worth about $34,000, into a Hyperliquid wallet and opened a bullish position tied to POPCAT, according to the complaint.

He closed that position at a profit after the token became available on Robinhood but before the company published its listing announcement, the FBI alleged. The complaint identified at least 10 other occasions through February 2026 when the same wallet traded ahead of announcements, including positions involving MEW, MOODENG, ONDO and RENDER.

Hyperliquid's perpetual futures let traders speculate on a cryptocurrency's price without owning the token itself. Unlike conventional futures, the contracts have no expiration date, and a “long” position gains value if the underlying token's price rises.

New listings can increase a token's exposure to buyers and put upward pressure on its price. Prosecutors said Xiang used his advance knowledge to position himself for those moves, sometimes closing his trades before the public knew Robinhood had added the asset.

“No matter the trading platform, corporate insiders will be held accountable when they trade based on misappropriated information,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in Monday's announcement.

Robinhood said in September that it had investigated the matter, reported it to authorities and maintained a zero-tolerance policy on insider trading.

Xiang faces a statutory maximum of 20 years in prison, although the judge will decide his sentence. He is scheduled to appear before McMahon for sentencing on February 25, 2027.

#4852. BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF snaps $2.35B outflow streak amid extreme fear

BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF ended 11 sessions of withdrawals totaling $2.35 billion, but CryptoQuant says one day of inflows is too early to signal a recovery.

BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) returned to inflows Monday, ending an 11-session outflow streak totaling roughly $2.35 billion.

The iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) attracted $76.5 million on Nov. 16, helping US spot Bitcoin ETFs record $7.9 million in net inflows despite withdrawals from several other funds, according to Farside Investors data.

The inflows came as Bitcoin (BTC) traded near multimonth lows of $64,000, while the Crypto Fear and Greed Index, which tracks cryptocurrency market sentiment, fell to 10 out of 100 on Monday, its lowest reading since June 2026.

Nick Pitto, head of marketing at blockchain analytics company CryptoQuant, cautioned against interpreting the inflows as a broader market recovery.

“One day of inflows doesn’t change the picture too much,” Pitto said. He noted that Monday’s inflows recovered only about 3% of IBIT’s withdrawals over the previous 11 sessions, while US Bitcoin ETFs had shed more than 31,000 BTC over the past month.

“It’s too early to call this dip buying,” he said, adding: “We’d need to see several days of inflows in a row, and from more funds than just BlackRock’s.”

Salman Parcy, managing partner at crypto investment company Cequire Capital, offered a more optimistic interpretation, suggesting that some institutional investors may see Bitcoin’s recent decline as a buying opportunity.

“While it is still early to call this a reversal, the return of capital to IBIT does show that some institutional investors are beginning to see an opportunity in current price levels,” Parcy said.

Related: Bitcoin price fails to hold $65K as US stocks drop further on AI nerves

Monday also marked the deadline for most institutions to file their third-quarter Form 13F disclosures, revealing Bitcoin ETF holdings as of Sept. 30. Several institutions reported increased exposure during the quarter, but Pitto cautioned against linking those holdings to Monday’s inflows.

“ETF buying peaked in August and September. But the filings only show what they held at the end of September, not what they’ve done since. So they may not explain Monday’s inflow,” he said.

#4851. Jenna Dewan Faced Criticism, a Partner Suspension, and a Shock Dancing with the Stars Exit. She’s Still Proud.

In an exclusive interview with Women’s Health, the actor reflects on her time in the ballroom.

Dancing with the Stars fans let out a collective gasp Tuesday night. Jenna Dewan and her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy, had earned one of the night’s top scores: 28 out of 30. They also won their dance-off against Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, tying for second on the leaderboard with Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov. Then host Alfonso Ribeiro called Dewan’s name, eliminating her from competition.

“I had a great time, and I loved getting to share that with the world,” she said, moments after being eliminated. “All love.”

Not even 48 hours later, Jenna sat down with Women’s Health to share her story.

Jenna Dewan: Overall, it’s really been the saying, “Two things can be true at once.” There's so many different emotions, and it's kind of hard to even put into words because obviously doing a show like this is such an enormous undertaking, and it's physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually intense. And so, when that's just finished, it's like a light switch goes off, and then you almost don't even know where you are.

I feel all kinds of things. I feel mostly proud. I feel really proud of myself, and I feel proud of the last dance we gave on the ballroom floor, and I feel obviously sad that it's over, that I don't get to give any more dances out there and create any more special pieces. So I think it's really both. I feel really proud of us, and I feel fulfilled, and I feel filled up, and I also feel sad that the journey of creating dances is over.

JD: When you are going through the show, it feels like any week could be you. The show is not necessarily a show about dance. It's not necessarily a competition about the best dancer. It's not about the best dance you give. It's so many other elements that go into it, which is great on a reality show front-end. It makes people tune in for all different kinds of reasons, but in doing that, you never know how it's going to go.

Once it started whittling down, it was the two of us. You kind of come to a place of like, “Okay, this could be our moment.” And I had a feeling—it was a tough week as far as some of the online noise, I would say, that goes with doing the show. So it definitely wasn't out of my mind that it could be a possibility.

Even before Jenna stepped onto the DWTS dance floor, viewers debated whether she belonged in the competition. How much prior dance experience a celebrity contestant can have—while still being considered a fair competitor—has long been a point of debate among viewers.

Jenna started her career as a dancer, where she toured alongside legendary performers, including Janet Jackson (she appeared in two music videos of the singer’s). In 2006, she landed her breakout role in Step Up, in which she played a classically trained ballerina. She was the host for television shows World of Dance and Flirty Dancing as well as a judge on Come Dance with Me. Many fans of DWTS cited Jenna’s impressive resume as an unfair advantage. “How is Jenna Dewan part of this? She was a professional dancer. Hello! So unfair already,” one X user wrote on the platform after the official season 35 cast announcement.

It should be noted, however, Jenna is not the first celebrity to join the show with previous dance experience—and it’s safe to say she’ll be far from the last. Stars like Heather Morris, Jordan Fisher, and Charli D’Amelio have all undergone criticism for joining the show in the past, despite having a substantial leg up among fellow contestants. Even Alfonso, the show’s current host and season 19 winner, had prior dance experience.

JD: I will say, through the history of watching the show and what I know about the show, is I've seen there be an issue with people with dance backgrounds, and that obviously there's a lot of opinions on whether we should even have people compete on the show that have dance backgrounds.

I definitely asked quite a few times, “Are you sure you guys want me on the show?” But the incredible people who do the show were really confident in expressing to me that this show had changed a lot, and that it’s not Dancing with the Stars Who Have Never Danced. They wanted a very dynamic cast with all different levels and strengths they bring to the ballroom. I knew it would be an uphill battle for me for sure, just from the patterns of the show and the loyalists of the show and how they feel. But ultimately, the gift of doing something just for myself was really intoxicating, and it won over any sort of doubts or hesitations I had.

JD: The hardest part of the show, I would say, is it really teaches you that joy and difficulty can exist together. There were so many highs of this journey, and then so many moments of frustration and negative noise and criticism that is honestly sad, because it tries to suck out the joy from the experience.

Even for myself with a dance background, it is vulnerable to put yourself out there in the ballroom every Tuesday and be like, “Hey guys, watch my dance and tell me what you think.” And then you have the whole other element of this social, online, noisy world that is almost like they're looking to tear people down, and I felt that that was an unfortunate shade to this show that didn't need to happen.

JD: Part of the journey of the show is interesting because for the first good couple weeks, you rarely see any of the other contestants, because you are really in your own rehearsal space, and you're just trying to get the dances down as fast as you can with your partner. I think it was rare seeing people in the hallways and connecting with some of the contestants. But yeah, we definitely would talk.

I think at one point Connor [Wood] made me laugh so hard because he said he had seen some of the online social negativity, and he said, “Everyone needs to go back to journaling.” I laughed so hard, because he is exactly right. At some point, we all thought it was okay to just get online and to be mean for no reason. We are real human beings that see this and feel this, and I think that that gets forgotten.

When we did the team dance, that was when we really were able to start bonding as the contestants, because we were finally together working towards one dance and in a room together. I absolutely love them, and we were all definitely talking about this and sharing our experiences with this, and how most of us at that point, I think, had taken it off our phone or turned off social media.

JD: Naturally, because of my dance background, there were really high expectations that I put on myself, and that the world was putting on me. I didn't even realize it was happening, but it was creating this feeling that I needed to let go of perfection and kind of just get comfortable being seen and just being there. I didn't need to prove anything.

I think I just realized how much of my life I spent wanting to get things right. And this experience really challenged me in that way, because what I realized is, you just can't grow if you're constantly worried about being perfect. I had to learn to be a little uncomfortable, to be critiqued again, to make some mistakes, to be vulnerable, and just let people see me in the middle of figuring something out. There's actually a lot of freedom in that, because I didn't have ballroom dance down perfectly by the time I got out there.

JD: I thought that every dance we did. I thought that during the week two jive, and it was intriguing to me that [the judges] were so critical of certain dances. However, when I look back, there was a lot of growth for me.

There was a whole element of this that was sort of discovering my strength in a new way because I have had three children, I've navigated huge life transitions, I've built a career, a family, a life, And now, I'm stepping into this show where I'm pushing myself physically, emotionally, creatively in a way that I haven't in years. So I think I just surprised myself with how strong I am, and not just physically, but emotionally.

Jenna also faced an unexpected complication when her partner, Val, was suspended for one episode of the show following a social media post he made about DWTS judge Carrie Ann Inaba. After Carrie Ann criticized his wife, fellow pro dancer Jenna Johnson, for including what she considered an illegal lift in her routine with Harry Shum Jr., Val posted, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The now-deleted post was widely interpreted as a reference to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after making a joke about his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith.

Carrie Ann appeared to interpret the post as a threat. She shared a screenshot of a Page Six story about it on Instagram, writing, “So this is what we are doing now?”

On Oct. 17, DWTS production company BBC Studios said Val would not participate in the Oct. 20 episode. Jenna danced with pro Alan Bersten in his place.

JD: I said this, and I really mean this, that I did not foresee having as many challenges as I did that were thrown at me during my Dancing with the Stars journey. However, the challenges of it gave me an opportunity to walk my talk, and I always think that when that happens, you can go back to your true north, to what’s your intention for doing something. How do you want to show up as a human when you’re experiencing challenges? And I kept going back to my kids. When the mid-season suspension happened, and all these things were going on, I thought, “I have a real opportunity here. I can be annoyed and bitter and upset about this, or I can show up with grace and love and joy and focus on the moment.”

That particular week was about my mom and my dedication to her. And she was in town, thrilled to have this dance with me, and thrilled to experience this moment. And I thought that this is something she's going to remember. We're all going to remember my family forever. Let's focus on that, and let's not worry about all of this that's going on.

JD: I’ve seen that, and I feel like with just life in general, even outside of Dancing with the Stars, that is absolutely something that most females have experienced. I think there's been a great change in our world, but I think for years upon years upon years, women have had a fight against misogyny and inherent bias. Women at times in life are just held to a different standard than men, and I think that that is a real reflection.

We're expected to be exceptional, but also humble and confident, but not too confident, skilled, but not struggling enough to earn praise. There's all this pressure on women. It feels like sometimes if a woman is strong or capable, the expectations become that much higher. I think people are so busy expecting women to be extraordinary that we forget to celebrate them for being extraordinary.

JD: It's never too late for a new chapter in life. And I think if there was like, one thing I wanted people to take away from my whole journey, it’s that we're never finished becoming who we are, and it's never too late to choose your own passion in life and your own joy in life. There isn't some age where you stop growing and dreaming and trying new things.

#4850. US senators seek SEC answers on tokenized stock money laundering risks

Four Democratic senators asked who would be responsible for tokenized shares transferred outside regulated platforms and whether the SEC could freeze or recover those tokens.

Four Democratic senators pressed the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to clarify financial crime safeguards under its tokenized stock exemption, warning that tokenized shares bought by verified investors could reach offshore or unverified wallets.

In a letter released Monday, Senators Angela Alsobrooks, Catherine Cortez Masto, Mark Warner and Ruben Gallego questioned how Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer rules apply to tokenized securities venues, which can trade certain US stocks without registering as securities exchanges.

The senators said the SEC’s Sept. 17 Innovation Exemption requires venues to control trading access but does not mandate restrictions on subsequent transfers. They asked who would be responsible for tokens moved outside of regulated platforms and whether the SEC could recover or freeze them.

The lawmakers also questioned issuers’ rights to object, retail investors’ access to best execution protections and custody safeguards. They asked SEC Chair Paul Atkins 13 questions, urging more transparent rulemaking and requesting answers within 30 days.

When announcing the exemption in September, Atkins said federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules would continue to apply in full.

OKXICE, a venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange, has also faced issuer objections. Its Nov. 5 public notice listed 67 companies that objected to their tokenized shares being traded on the venue.

Separately, crypto exchange Backpack said Monday that it had secured Commodity Futures Trading Commission approval to establish a US derivatives exchange and clearinghouse using blockchain infrastructure, paving the way for leveraged crypto perpetual futures trading.

CFTC Chair Michael Selig said blockchain-based operators must meet the same regulatory standards as traditional firms, including AML, customer protection and market surveillance requirements.

Backpack also has a tokenized equities business, although its latest CFTC approvals concern derivatives rather than the SEC exemption questioned by lawmakers.

#4849. Binance Hack Wallets Move $137 Million in Ethereum After Two Weeks of Silence

Binance Hack Wallets Move $137 Million in Ethereum After Two Weeks of Silence

Wallets linked to the $6.3 billion Binance hack started moving large amounts of stolen Ethereum on Tuesday, breaking more than two weeks of inactivity as U.S. authorities continue trying to recover the funds.

Blockchain security service MistTrack reported that one address associated with the October 29 theft sent 34,279.66 ETH, worth roughly $63 million at the time, to three newly created wallets. The address had not moved its funds since October 30.

The on-chain record shows three outgoing transactions shortly before 7 a.m. UTC: two transfers of 12,000 ETH ($21.2 million) each and a third of about 10,279.66 ETH ($18.2 million). MistTrack said the receiving wallets had not sent the ether onward when it posted its initial alert.

That $63 million movement was only part of Tuesday’s activity. A second wallet linked to the same hack transferred another 40,600.66 ETH, worth roughly $74 million, across five transactions.

Analytics firm Arkham shows wallets linked to the attack had transferred a combined 74,880 ETH, valued at $136.8 million, over roughly three hours, and funds were beginning to be swapped for Bitcoin through Thorchain, a service that moves and exchanges crypto between blockchains.

The transfers come five days after the Justice Department said courts had authorized it to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion connected to the Binance theft. That sum is part of more than $2.7 billion frozen through combined government and private-sector action, not an additional recovery on top of it.

The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a hacking operation it links to North Korea’s military. The October 29 breach drained roughly $6.43 billion from Binance across 11 blockchains, according to blockchain analytics company Elliptic, making it the largest known crypto theft. North Korea denied involvement.

The attackers rushed to convert stablecoins into assets their issuers could not freeze. Tether and Circle can block stolen tokens on their networks, but ordinary ETH and Bitcoin do not have a central company capable of stopping a particular wallet from sending them.

Elliptic’s November 16 analysis put the frozen or seized portion at $2.85 billion and said the main Bitcoin and ETH holdings were still sitting in attack-linked addresses. That was before Tuesday’s transfers, which show at least part of the previously stationary ETH has begun moving.

The attackers had also spread their activity across almost 27,000 wallets and more than 83,000 transactions. That complicated trail does not mean they have managed to turn most of the stolen assets into cash.

Elliptic said only a negligible amount had likely been cashed out as of its latest assessment. To do that at scale, the holders would typically need an exchange or an over-the-counter broker willing to take the funds, creating another point at which authorities could identify and potentially block them.
