#4848. Jensen Huang’s Houses: Exploring the Former Nvidia CEO’s $38 Million San Francisco Mansion and Other Properties

It’s been a big week for Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang. The billionaire announced he is stepping down as CEO of the AI hardware giant following reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs: one with a suspected Chinese spy, and another with one of his company’s senior executives (other reports allege a third affair with another Nvidia employee). Huang will reportedly testify before Congress later this month to discuss his relationship with the alleged spy. We can only assume that the Taipei City native is weathering the storm at home, but where are Jensen Huang’s houses? Even Huang himself may be wondering about the answer to that question, if a recent New York Times interview is any indication (more on that later).

Unsurprisingly, the tech titan hasn’t strayed too far from Silicon Valley, where Nvidia has been based since it was founded in the mid-’80s, with his real estate purchases. After graduating from Oregon State University, where he met his wife, Lori Huang, Huang began buying properties in California’s Bay Area, and he and Lori still own two of them. So far, the superbillionaire’s only exception to that rule has been an estate on Maui in Hawaii. Time will tell if the scandal spurs any real estate changes for him.

One thing that will presumably change about Huang’s home life in the immediate future: footing the bill for his security team. Nvidia has, until now, covered the cost of its former CEO’s private security. The company spent about $4 million in 2026 on “home security, protection during personal travel, consulting, and drivers” for Huang, per the New York Post. Though that arrangement is likely coming to an end, that shouldn’t be too big a problem for Jensen; the scandal has put Nvidia’s stock—and therefore Jensen’s net worth—in a slight flux, but he is still worth an estimated $144.7 billion at the time of publication.

Read on for a rundown of Jensen Huang’s houses dating back to his arrival in Silicon Valley.

According to The New York Times, Huang married Lori shortly after his 1984 graduation from Oregon State University, where they met as lab partners in an electrical engineering class. The newlywed graduates hightailed it to Silicon Valley to start their careers as microchip designers, and Jensen bought his first house: a 1,500-square-foot three-bedroom home in San Jose, California. It’s unclear exactly when or for how much he bought the property, but Jensen sold it in 1988 for $185,000.

That same year, Huang and Lori moved into a larger San Jose home that they bought for $338,000. With 2,300 square feet of interior living space, it had four bedrooms. Huang lived here when he co-founded Nvidia in 1993; he sold the house in 2002 for $500,000, the Wall Street Journal reports.

From there, the Huangs moved into an even more upgraded residence: a 7,000-square-foot home in Los Altos Hills, a tony area about 15 miles from the Nvidia headquarters. They paid $6.9 million for the newly built six-bedroom dwelling in 2003. According to Realtor.com, the two-story house hosts a resort-worthy swimming pool. The Huangs still own this house.

A year after buying his house in Los Altos Hills, Huang paid $7.5 million for a Hawaiian estate. The oceanfront property is located within Wailea Resort, an exclusive gated community on the south side of Maui, per the Wall Street Journal. The contemporary-style mansion reportedly has seven bedrooms across about 8,000 square feet. The Huangs still maintain this residence too.

In 2017, Huang made his most recent real estate purchase: a newly completed $38 million mansion in the high-end Pacific Heights neighborhood on San Francisco’s Gold Coast. The residence is modern in style, with a curved roofline and a limestone exterior. It boasts 11,400 square feet of interior living space, with seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms, three half-baths, a wine cellar, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a home theater, a gym with a sauna, a library, numerous fireplaces, and a fifth-floor observation deck with views of the Golden Gate Bridge. The house took four years to construct, its developer told the WSJ.

San Francisco’s famous Golden Gate Bridge.

This seems to be Huang’s primary residence—although, according to a September 2026 New York Times interview, he could not tell you where it is. “There are a lot of skills that don’t matter,” Huang told the outlet in response to a question about AI weakening students’ basic math skills. “My first confession, I actually don’t know my address.… One day I had to pump gas—it was a few years ago. They needed my ZIP code, and I panicked. I didn’t know my ZIP code. I don’t know my telephone number. I forget these things. I can live with it.”

“Having your name on a shirt or bib is soooo fun because even strangers will cheer you on along the course! I’m less anxious knowing that I’ll be able to get in touch with people and that my phone is good to go. “I keep it on my bathroom counter so I don’t forget to swipe at minimum inner thighs and inner arms for a training run. #4846. Revolut plans four blockchain-based funds for private markets, chair says

Citing a looming liquidity crunch, Martin Gilbert said blockchain could help bring more liquidity to private markets.

Revolut plans to launch four funds using blockchain to offer fractional investments in illiquid markets, chair Martin Gilbert said Tuesday at Solana’s Breakpoint conference in London.

Blockchain, he explained, would be used to divide funds focused on illiquid markets “into what I would term marketable sizes.”

“If you want to buy a private equity fund on Revolut going forward, when we do launch these funds, you will be able to buy them in fractional amounts.”

The company, which has said it has over 80 million customers worldwide, launched a private market investment platform to eligible customers in Europe in July. Managed by a number of firms including Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group, the funds already on the platform allow for a minimum investment of 1 euro.

Warning that the financial sector may be entering into a liquidity crunch, particularly in private markets, he highlighted the need to attract more buyers to these markets, which blockchains could facilitate.

“In this world, there is liquidity until there is no liquidity,” he said. “If you can help people get liquidity in illiquid assets, you’re going to solve a lot of problems for a lot of people. The only way you can do that is to be blockchain enabled.”

The company hasn’t yet released details on the blockchain-based funds or when they will launch.

#4845. Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as Nvidia CEO, publicly addressing the campaign to reinstate him less than a week after his abrupt departure. His offer came despite reports that the chipmaker's board has no plans to bring him back.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote in a statement on X.

The Nvidia co-founder also apologized for the conduct that triggered his exit. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he wrote. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.”

“I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he added.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…

— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026

His X profile underwent a separate change around the same time. By Tuesday, Huang had removed “CEO” from his bio, which now identifies him only as “Founder of NVIDIA”; the company banner and corporate affiliation badge also disappeared.

Huang resigned last Thursday after 33 years leading the chipmaker he founded in 1993. His departure followed disclosures about extramarital relationships involving Nvidia employees and a business executive whom U.S. officials suspect of connections to Chinese intelligence. Those intelligence allegations have not been established as fact.

The board's independent investigation is examining his conduct and whether sensitive company information or national security were put at risk. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised; chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. He said many were reaching out directly as Nvidia navigates “complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” he added.

But the board's position—at least as of Tuesday—is that directors are focused on the investigation, not reinstatement.

The company is simultaneously looking for a successor. Directors reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive, according to the Financial Times, although Nvidia said it had not formally engaged candidates and called speculation premature.

The movement to restore Huang has nevertheless attracted powerful allies. President Donald Trump said Monday he “would certainly not mind” a comeback, while Elon Musk backed a petition demanding Huang's reinstatement that had drawn nearly 192,000 signatures by Monday.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman offered a more qualified defense. Altman, who was briefly fired and reinstated at OpenAI in 2023, said Huang had “long been a hero of mine” and that “heroes have flaws,” but stopped short of saying Nvidia should rehire him.

Huang also made a patriotic appeal, especially considering his outsting was especially rushed not because of his affairs but because of the possibility of him leaking secrets to China. “I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life,” he wrote.

“NVIDIA has been my life’s work,” he continued. “Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.”

He closed by thanking supporters and telling his family, “I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.” Nvidia, meanwhile, is continuing its permanent CEO search, with Kress scheduled to lead the company's quarterly earnings call later today.

Surrounded by trees, this small wooden house in Denmark blends seamlessly with nature.

Named the EcoNeo House, the home was designed by the Danish architectural firm SAGA Space Architects, both as a family home and as a prototype for tiny house-style vacation homes. Although originally conceived as a summer house, the cottage has been insulated and heated, allowing it to be used even during colder weather. At only 377 square feet, it combines the essential features of a vacation home, sleeping up to six people. The design prioritizes a thoughtful use of the available space and forward-thinking architecture that blends into the landscape.

The spacious terrace is perfect for sunbathing and dining outdoors, especially in the summer.

Inside, the living and dining areas flow seamlessly into one another. Thanks to the large windows that offer views of the surrounding trees, there’s a connection between indoors and outdoors. The kitchen is set slightly apart, but opens up into the dining area, blending smoothly into the floor plan. The dining area flows seamlessly into the kitchen. Additional storage space was created below the stairs on the left, which lead to the sleeping lofts.

The choice of materials complements the understated architecture. The floor’s wide Douglas fir planks introduce a warm color and vibrant grain. The use of wood is consistently carried through to other areas of the house, creating a visual connection between the living space and the sauna. Natural materials are also used in the bathroom, including Kolmården marble, a Swedish stone distinguished by its characteristic green hue.

Wood defines the interior and lends the rooms a natural warmth. Large windows bring the surrounding nature into the home, while the dining area is spacious even within the compact layout.

Together with the stones and the greenery outside, the result is a design that deliberately avoids contrasts and excess. “When designing the summer house, every detail was intended to reflect the harmony between sustainable innovation and timeless craftsmanship,” explains Niklas Munk-Andersen, architect and partner at SAGA Space Architects.

Beanbag chairs provide extra seating and blend harmoniously into the interior with their colors.

The bathroom features natural materials and Swedish marble finishes.

The sauna can also be converted into a sleeping area for two additional guests.

The boundary between indoors and outdoors blurs, bringing nature into focus.

This approach not only simplified assembly but also minimized the impact on the site.

Thanks to its small footprint, this vacation home’s emissions are 83% lower than those of the average vacation home that can accommodate six people. In addition, the modular construction minimizes the impact on the natural environment.

The EcoNeo House demonstrates that sustainable construction isn’t just a matter of the materials used. The size of a building and how the available space is utilized also play a crucial role. Though it may sound small, 377 square feet can be perfectly sufficient for a getaway home—provided the floor plan, storage space, and amenities are all carefully designed.

Although primarily intended as a summer home, this small vacation home can also be enjoyed in colder months.

A skylight lets light into the upper sleeping lofts.

The small vacation home has two separate sleeping lofts accommodating four people.

#4841. Bitcoin to $1M by 2030? ‘Almost certainly not,’ says Dragonfly’s Qureshi

Dragonfly’s Haseeb Qureshi says Bitcoin could reach $400,000 by 2030 but doubts it will return to $100,000 by year-end with the rout in AI stocks weighing on crypto.

Bitcoin is unlikely to reach $1 million by 2030 — though it could reach $400,000 — according to Dragonfly managing partner Haseeb Qureshi.

“The amount of capital that would have to come into crypto to get to million-dollar Bitcoin is an astronomical sum,” Qureshi tells Cointelegraph’s Trade Secrets. “The idea that you could get that amount of capital in five years or four years is just not plausible.”

A former professional poker player and software engineer at Airbnb, Qureshi now backs crypto startups at Dragonfly, which launched a $650 million fund in February.

Qureshi also says he doubts Bitcoin will return to six figures by year-end, linking the current crypto sell-off to the rout in AI stocks.

Nvidia (NVDA) shares closed 4.3% lower on Thursday after the chipmaker announced co-founder Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO following a series of scandals. Huang reportedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing denied the espionage allegation and President Donald Trump has expressed doubts too.

Nvidia is the leading AI chip supplier and accounted for 4.66% of the MSCI All Country World Index at the end of October, second only to Apple.

Bitcoin fell alongside Nvidia shares in the week Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. Source: TradingView

“Crypto is not the main story this year for financial markets,” Qureshi says. “Crypto is downstream of these other stories.”

Qureshi says investors grew concerned after Democrat sweep in the US midterms that new data centers would be harder to get approved. With high oil prices and inflation already weighing on the economy, the prospect of weaker AI investment prompted investors to cut exposure to riskier assets, including Bitcoin, he says.

Related: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT

That leaves crypto “largely along for the ride” through the year-end.

Crypto has spent much of 2026 in a bear market despite Bitcoin’s 43% recovery in the third quarter. Bitcoin traded near $65,000 on Monday, almost 50% below its October 2025 all-time high.

Bitcoin is far away from its $126,080 all-time high recorded in October 2025. Source: CoinGecko

The US Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act in September, stalling the industry’s push for federal rules for crypto markets. In October, suspected North Korean hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance in the largest crypto theft on record.

Over the next 15 to 20 years, Qureshi says Bitcoin could compete with gold as a store of value outside government control.

New deposits or advances in mining could add to the supply of gold, he says while Bitcoin’s protocol caps its supply at 21 million units.

“There will never be an asteroid that you will find a bunch of Bitcoin on.”

However, Qureshi sees a risk that AI could discover a flaw in the mathematics that secures Bitcoin transactions.

Bitcoin uses digital signatures to verify that a transaction was signed with the corresponding private key. If a future mathematical breakthrough makes it possible to forge those signatures, attackers could move coins without their owners’ permission.

Such a threat is often discussed alongside quantum computing risks. A powerful quantum computer could derive a private key from its corresponding public key using Shor’s algorithim, putting coins with public keys visible at risk of theft, which includes some of Satoshi Nakamoto’s early holdings.

Related: Nearly 10% of Bitcoin supply is ‘structurally unsafe’ from quantum breakthrough: Glassnode

In October, OpenAI said one of its models had found a faster way to solve certain logic problems, challenging a conjecture known as the Exponential Time Hypothesis.

Qureshi says a future AI-assisted discovery could break the cryptography Bitcoin uses to verify who can spend coins, undermining its case as a store of value.

“That, I think, is what you should price in as the chance this all breaks, this all fails,” he says.

Dragonfly has a history of backing innovative projects, and led stablecoin project Ethena’s $6 million seed round in 2023. Ethena had about $4.9 billion of its dollar-linked USDe token outstanding at the end of September. The protocol uses derivatives to offset price swings in the assets backing USDe. Some of the income those positions generate goes to users who stake the token.

Users who stake Venice’s VVV token can mint DIEM, which they can stake for daily credits to run AI models.

#4840. Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade threatens to break as many as 15,000 smart contracts, developers warned during a core developer call Monday, forcing a debate over how much disruption the network should tolerate in the name of scaling.

The concern centers on two proposed changes, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, designed to let Ethereum scale from 60 million gas to as much as 200 million gas per block, a roughly 3.3x jump that developers say would sharply lower costs for most users while keeping state growth in check.

The problem, flagged late in the development process, is that the changes break certain invariants, assumptions that some smart contracts were built to rely on.

“Multiple contracts were relying on invariants in the protocol that are modified by 8037 and 8038,” said Marius van der Wijden, an Ethereum Foundation developer who worked on the scaling effort.

He acknowledged that the team “wanted to do significant public outreach” but that timelines slipped amid reorganizations and budget cuts at the foundation. He said he shares “a lot of blame” as the last remaining scaling lead still at the EF.

Two security firms, ChainSecurity and Dedaub, presented findings from AI-assisted audits, with the combined search turning up roughly 200 distinct classes of affected contracts, most tied to gas-cost increases rather than the new mechanics themselves.

Van der Wijden put the highest estimate at 10,000 to 15,000 contracts, a “fringe subset” of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million, with impacted value he loosely pegged in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars among contracts not yet committed to upgrading.

App developers pushed back on the framing. Jango, who builds the Juicebox protocol, warned the change undermines “composability,” a core Ethereum value prop, and shakes “developer confidence in building immutable protocols.” A Uniswap developer urged that EIP-8037 “should definitely be reconsidered.”

The Ethereum Foundation already delayed Glamsterdam’s testnet fork over these gas-related security flaws. Developers stressed Monday that no decision has been made, with the question headed to Thursday’s execution-layer call.

But several signaled a strong desire to ship the fork as planned, arguing that removing the changes could delay Glamsterdam, and the broader roadmap toward post-quantum security, by four to six months, time they say Ethereum can’t spare as quantum and AI threats loom.

#4839. 007 Off Duty: 10 Photos of Former James Bond Actors at Home

For a secret agent, James Bond generates a remarkable amount of public discussion. Barely a day goes by without fresh speculation about who will be the next actor to take on the role of 007. Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor are among the names linked to the role, with recent reports suggesting the search has reached final screen tests.

Whoever takes over will join the small group who have played the part since Sean Connery’s debut in Dr. No in 1962. Away from the screen, the homes of these former James Bond actors reveal more about the men in the dinner jackets. These archival photographs find them settling into family life and indulging interests that occasionally followed them onto set. Below, find a little domestic distraction while we wait for the next Bond to introduce himself.

Sean Connery relaxing in his ground-floor basement flat in NW5.

Photographed at home in England in 1955, Connery is still around seven years away from his first appearance as James Bond in this shapshot. His surroundings are modest, with little suggestion of the polished interiors his screen alter ego was about to frequent. Connery established the role of Bond across six films in during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Landing the role of James Bond required a little wardrobe planning on George Lazenby’s part. According to the official Bond website, the former model bought an unused suit made for Connery, then visited his predecessor’s barber at the Dorchester to request the same haircut. Producer Cubby Broccoli happened to be in the neighboring chair.

George Lazenby pictured at his home in Kensington, London, 1973.

His only appearance as 007 was in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret Service. It gave Bond one of his most personal storylines, with Diana Rigg playing his ill-fated bride, Tracy. By the time of the Kensington photograph shown above in February 1973, Lazenby had already left the role. Seated with papers in hand, he is surrounded by books, records and a guitar propped beside the sofa. The glass-topped coffee table is crowded with objects, including a decorative horse’s head, while a substantial wooden cabinet provides storage behind him. Later that year, Roger Moore made his Bond debut in Live and Let Die.

Roger Moore reading the dictionary at his home in Los Angeles, circa 1955.

Roger Moore had yet to order his first on-screen Bond martini when he was photographed at home reading a dictionary, while working as a television actor.

Roger Moore kissing his wife, Welsh singer Dorothy Squires, outside their home in Bexley Heath, London, in 1957.

He married Welsh singer Dorothy Squires in 1953, and they lived primarily at The Mount—a mansion on Wansunt Road in Old Bexley, Kent.

The couple divorced in 1968, and a year later, Moore married Luisa Mattioli. Sherwood House in Denham, located close to Pinewood Studios, served as the couple's base during Moore's first three Bond films. In his autobiography, he described the property as “near London and perfect for a growing family.”

Its appeal extended to 11 acres of grounds, which included a tennis court, heated swimming pool and greenhouses when the house was advertised for £5 million in 2015.

When he finally took on Bond's on-screen persona, Timothy Dalton was well-prepared for the role.

Producers considered Timothy Dalton for Bond early in his career, but he felt too young for the role. When he eventually signed on for The Living Daylights in 1986, he reread Fleming’s novels to prepare for a more serious interpretation of the character.

Pierce Brosnan at home in Los Angeles in 1983.

Pierce Brosnan was making his name in Remington Steele when he posed at his Los Angeles home in June 1983, but his introduction to the world of Bond had come through his first wife, actress Cassandra Harris. She appeared in For Your Eyes Only, and visiting her on location in Corfu brought him into the producers’ orbit. Brosnan was offered the role in 1986, but was prevented from taking it due to his television commitments at the time. His debut in GoldenEye came almost a decade later, in 1995.

Pierce Brosnan playing pool with his son, Sean, at their Los Angeles home in 1992.

This 1992 photographs show Brosnan playing guitar on the sofa, shooting pool with his eight-year-old son Sean, and entertaining two dogs in the garden. Cream sofas and floral upholstery adorn the living room, while arched windows and white shutters open the space to the surrounding greenery. Taken the year after Harris died of ovarian cancer, the photographs capture Brosnan bringing up their family before Bond transformed his career.

Pierce Brosnan with his dogs outside of their Los Angeles home in 1992.

Painting had become a creative outlet for the star during Harris’s illness. Having trained as a commercial artist before acting, Brosnan returned to it in the late 1980s, recalling on his website: “I started painting again and out came every colour.” By the time he became Bond, painting was so sufficiently embedded in his life that his dressing room at Leavesden doubled as a studio during GoldenEye.

Daniel Craig attends the Bond 25 film launch at Ian Fleming's Home, GoldenEye, in Montego Bay, Jamaica, 2019.

For this final entry, the front door stays closed. Of all the former James Bond actors, Daniel Craig represents a more guarded approach to sharing domestic life. His wife, actress Rachel Weisz, explained the couple’s position in a 2012 conversation with British Vogue: “I think it’s pretty ordinary to think that marriage is private and sacred.”

Speculation over who will inherit Craig's martini glass keeps his name in the headlines even after his departure.

#4838. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4837. This Common Drug Was Just Linked to a 24% Lower Risk of Dementia

For all of the havoc dementia causes to a person's life, scientists are still trying to figure out exactly how to prevent it. While keeping your brain and body active and following a healthy diet seems to help, there doesn't seem to be a pill you can pop to lower your risk of developing the devastating disease. But new research suggests that a common osteoporosis drug might be worth investigating further.

It's a class of medications called nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (or NBPs). While these are typically used to strengthen bones in people with osteoporosis, NBPs could have the added benefit of supporting brain health as you age, too.

It's important to stress this now: The researchers found a link between people who used NBPs and a lower risk of dementia, but they didn't prove that the medications themselves actually dropped the risk. Still, doctors say there could be something to this. "The association is intriguing," says Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

Here's what experts want you to take away from the findings.

Meet the experts: Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong; Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California; and Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

The study, which was published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, analyzed the electronic medical records of more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older in Hong Kong. All of the participants had osteoporosis or fractures due to fragility (meaning, their bones had weakened).

Researchers discovered that people who took NBPs had a 16 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared to those who didn't take medication for osteoporosis. But when they compared those who used NBPs to those taking other types of osteoporosis medications, the dementia risk was 24 percent lower.

The link seemed to be especially strong in women and patients who had hip fractures.

The researchers were inspired to look into NBPs and Alzheimer’s because the drug had been shown to improve cognitive function in previous animal models of neurotoxicity and Alzheimer’s disease, says Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong. “These findings led us to investigate whether their use might also be associated with a lower risk of dementia in humans."

While the study didn't prove that NBPs were responsible for the lowered risk, doctors have a few theories on what could be driving this.

For one, it’s possible that the link is more indirect, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California. NBPs improve bone density over time, which allows people to be more active, Dr. Segil says. "Broken bones do not cause dementia but do decrease activity," he says. (Being sedentary is a risk factor for dementia.)

There may also be something about NBPs themselves that could lower the risk of dementia, though. "Some researchers speculate that these medications could influence inflammation, immune pathways, or other biological processes involved in neurodegeneration," Dr. Hoehler says. But, she points out, more research is needed.

For now, doctors don't plan to prescribe NBPs in an effort to lower dementia risk. But Dr. Cheung says it should make people feel confident about using this class of medication for bone health. "Given the low uptake of osteoporosis treatment, people with osteoporosis should consider appropriate anti-osteoporosis medication, which may offer an additional benefit for brain health," he says. Even though osteoporosis drugs are commonly available, uptake has been historically low—studies have previously estimated that around seven percent of women with osteoporosis actually take medication for it.

Ultimately, doctors say that a clinical trial is needed to see if NBPs actually lower the risk of dementia. "If future studies confirm these results, they could open an exciting new avenue for Alzheimer's prevention or treatment," Dr. Hoehler says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. #4835. Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold roughly $85 million worth of Nvidia shares Monday while buying close to $40 million in crypto-exposed stocks, rebalancing exposure to technology and fintech stocks during a broad selloff.

The firm's daily trade file for November 16 shows sales of 543,092 Nvidia shares across two actively managed exchange-traded funds. Using Monday's $156.14 closing price, those shares were worth approximately $84.8 million; the disclosures list share counts rather than the exact prices ARK received.

ARK bought 277,523 shares of payments company Block, worth about $23 million at the close. It also added 180,534 shares of stablecoin issuer Circle, valued at $10.4 million, and 53,760 shares of crypto exchange Coinbase, worth around $6.4 million.

The purchases were spread across funds rather than concentrated in one vehicle. ARK's flagship Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought Circle and most of the Block shares, while its Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW) bought Coinbase and the remaining Block stock.

All three crypto-linked stocks fell Monday. Circle dropped 7.3%, Coinbase declined 6.1% and Block lost 1.9%, while Nvidia slid 4.1% as investors continued selling technology shares.

That makes the whole movement seem like a shift in holdings, not evidence that ARK expects cryptocurrencies to recover before AI stocks. The manager says its funds can rebalance every trading day, and its trade notifications don't disclose why each position was changed or establish that particular sales financed particular purchases.

ARK had bought 90,443 Nvidia shares just one week earlier, on November 9, during another selloff. The latest sale therefore reverses some of that buying without necessarily suggesting the firm has abandoned the chipmaker or its long-standing investment case for artificial intelligence.

ARK also purchased 378,515 shares of SpaceX, worth roughly $52 million, while selling 30,659 shares of crypto exchange Bullish and units of Ethereum and Solana staking funds. So in this case, Wood would be selling crypto to buy one single AI stock.

Those sales included 300,000 shares of the 3iQ Ethereum Staking ETF and 350,000 shares of the 3iQ Solana Staking ETF. The firm's buying of crypto companies coincided with cuts to other crypto-related investments, a distinction that matters when trying to read a trading strategy from one day's activity.

Wood has repeatedly bought companies that handle crypto trading and payments during market selloffs. In September, ARK bought $37 million in Block stock in one session, and it previously increased its Circle and Coinbase stakes while reducing exposure to other crypto names.

The companies offer different ways to invest in digital assets without holding tokens directly. Block runs Cash App and Bitcoin-related products; Circle issues the USDC dollar-backed stablecoin; and Coinbase, the only American crypto exchange listed on the stock market, earns revenue from cryptocurrency trading and other services.

ARK's strategy has never been a simple choice between crypto and AI. Its flagship fund already counted Circle, Coinbase and SpaceX among major positions in August, alongside businesses tied to artificial intelligence and financial technology, as earlier holdings showed.

Nvidia's leadership changed five days before Monday's trades. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 11, with finance chief Colette Kress appointed interim chief executive, according to the company's SEC filing.

The chipmaker is due to report fiscal third-quarter results after the market closes Tuesday, with a conference call at 5 p.m. Eastern. Those results will give investors their first earnings update since the leadership change—one day after ARK sold more than half a million shares.

#4834. ‘I Picked Up Weights for the First Time in My Mid-50s. I Was Powerlifting by My 70s—Here’s How’

“Getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it.”

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If I’ve learned anything over the past few years, it’s to just say yes. Saying the word was simple, but ended up changing my relationship with fitness—and transforming my whole life.

I’ve always loved being physically active and moving my body; I ran track and field in high school, played field hockey in both high school and college, and enjoyed horseback riding as a young adult. But shortly after graduating, I had my first of seven children at 23. From that point on, I went straight into parenting mode: My family became my priority, and with so much to juggle, exercise took a back seat for the next few decades.

But at 55, I wanted to feel strong in my body again. My kids were grown and I had more free time, so I signed up for a gym membership. I even started working with a personal trainer to make sure I was doing the right moves safely. Over the next 15 years, I exercised with several trainers, lifting light weights once or twice a week with dumbbells and weight machines. I enjoyed the workouts and saw improvements to my overall fitness, but I wasn’t particularly passionate about going to the gym, so I wasn’t always consistent and never set any real goals.

Then, at 70, everything changed. My trainer who I had come to enjoy working with and trust moved away, and without that connection, I stopped going to the gym. But after about a year away, the fitness manager at my gym, Nate Fleming, reached out to me, and I began working with him twice a week.

He immediately changed up my programming and introduced me to the idea of progressive overload. I learned that gradually increasing the weight I lifted each week could help me build muscle, get stronger, and see real results. He also added new movements to my routine, like farmer’s carries, deadlifts, and squat variations. Deadlifts, in particular, became one of my favorite exercises—I loved that the move required so much technique. There was something so satisfying about picking up a heavy weight and realizing I could lift more than I thought.

Nearly overnight, my attitude toward fitness changed: I enjoyed being challenged and discovering how much stronger I could become when I pushed myself. Over the next year, I began to see visible muscle definition in my arms and legs and felt more energized throughout the day. More importantly, though, my confidence skyrocketed because I had developed a greater trust in my own abilities.

I had grown to love lifting heavy, and wanted to step outside my comfort zone and discover what I could accomplish in my 70s. I casually asked Nate if there were deadlifting competitions for older women, and he said there were. So, I took a leap of faith and started a seven-month training process for a powerlifting competition (which took place this past March). I upped my training to three days a week, continuing to progressively increase the weights, and worked on refining my technique to move more efficiently.

The day of the competition was one of the best days of my life. I decided to compete in all three lifts: I squatted 132 pounds, bench-pressed 71.5 pounds, and deadlifted 242 pounds, setting records in all three lifts for my age and weight category in Nova Scotia, Canada, where I live. I was so proud of what I’d accomplished and felt incredibly empowered by what my body could do at 71. My kids and grandkids were also there to cheer me on, which made the day even more special. Sharing that moment with my family and showing them what was possible at my age meant so much to me. I walked away feeling stronger, more confident, and excited to do it again.

My next powerlifting competition is this month, and I still lift with Nate three days a week. My training is structured in four-week blocks, and the weight, sets, and reps change each week. For instance, in week one, I might do 3 sets of 5 reps at a moderate weight. Then, I gradually increase the load in weeks two and three while lowering the reps as I get closer to my heaviest lifts. Week four is a deload week, so I reduce the weight and give my body a chance to recover before lifting heavier again.

Each workout starts with the main lift (deadlift, squat, or bench press) because that’s when I have the most energy. Then, I move on to three or four accessory exercises, where I use lighter weights to strengthen supporting muscles, address weaknesses, and improve my performance in the main lifts. For example, on deadlift day, I might incorporate exercises like lunges, hamstring curls, and bent-over rows to strengthen my glutes, hamstrings, and back.

I’m incredibly proud of my progress over the last six months. I have a lingering shoulder injury, so right now, my bench press has stayed about the same at 71.5 pounds. But I can squat 160 pounds and deadlift 265 pounds, which is only five pounds away from the Canadian deadlift record.

While I train hard, I recover even harder in between sessions. I get seven to eight hours of sleep each night and am mindful about nutrition, eating lots of protein, since it’s important for building and maintaining muscle. I aim for around 120 grams a day, with eggs, chicken, and fish as some of my go-to sources. Additionally, during rest days, I focus on stretching and hip and shoulder mobility to improve my range of motion. I don’t count my steps, but I try to walk as much as I can throughout the day to keep my body moving and maintain cardiovascular health.

I love Feetures socks for their snug arch support and gentle compression that keeps them comfortably in place during workouts.

Clif Builders are my favorite post-workout snack since they taste great and pack 20 g of protein per bar.

When I first decided to work with a personal trainer in my 50s, I wanted guidance, accountability, and the confidence that I was exercising safely and effectively—and I got that. My first few trainers helped me build a foundation by teaching me proper form and the fundamental movements that I still rely on today.

But working with Nate completely changed my relationship with lifting: He knows how to motivate me, pushing me without going beyond my abilities. When I attempt a new personal record, his belief in me helps me believe in myself, too. Now, I know what I’m capable of and how to challenge myself while lifting safely. The gym has become so much more than a place to work out—it’s where I keep discovering what I can do.

I’ve learned that getting stronger isn’t just about how hard I work in the gym—it’s also about how well I recover between workouts through getting plenty of sleep, mobility work, stretching, and walking. When I don’t make time for recovery activities or I don’t fuel properly, it makes a difference; I feel more fatigued, have less energy during workouts, and struggle to perform at the same level.

For me, progress doesn’t mean pushing myself to the limit every day. It means finding the right balance between challenging my body and giving it the rest and support it needs to keep getting stronger.

If you’d told me a few years ago that I’d be powerlifting in my 70s and chasing a deadlift record, I never would have believed you. Before I started training with Nate, I had never really set big fitness goals or thought about pushing my limits. But that began to change when I realized how much stronger I could become with the right coaching and encouragement. I was inspired to set goals that challenged me in new ways I never thought possible, and I’ve learned that it’s never too late to surprise myself and try something new. Having a goal to work toward keeps me motivated, and I love seeing how far I can push myself when I have the right support and plan in place.

Of course, getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it. I hope my journey encourages other women, especially those in their 60s and 70s, to keep challenging themselves and try new things. They might discover a passion they never knew they had, just as I did.

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. #4831. Bitcoin Investors Are Capitulating—That’s Historically Been a Bottom Signal

Bitcoin Investors Are Capitulating—That’s Historically Been a Bottom Signal

Bitcoin’s latest crash has pushed investors into the kind of loss-taking that has historically shown up near market bottoms.

Realized losses, which investors lock in when they sell coins for less than they paid, have climbed relative to the profits taken over the past year.

That measure now sits at levels seen only near the lows of 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023, according to a report published Tuesday by onchain analytics firm Glassnode. It’s the first such reading since then.

Most of the selling came from recent buyers. Holders of coins less than six months old took losses into early 2026, cashed in gains during the rally into September and October, and are now selling at a loss again, Glassnode said. Leverage has been flushed too, with Nov. 13 and 14 bringing some of the largest long liquidations relative to open interest since 2023.

Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Nov. 15 before bouncing, and it traded near $64,970 on Tuesday. More than $2 billion in liquidations over the weekend left traders watching $60,000 as a potential next stop, Decrypt reported. The slide deepened last week as fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes erased Bitcoin’s summer rally. Rising interest rates generally do not bode well for risk assets like Bitcoin, since investors typically rotate to safer bets like U.S. Treasuries when rates elevate.

But there are early signs of support, according to Glassnode. Buyers absorbed about 66,000 BTC in the $62,000 to $66,000 range during the two days of heaviest selling, adding to a zone where recent buyers accumulated around the August low.

Resting bids on Binance and Coinbase within 5% of the price now outweigh asks by about 2.3 to 1. The Coinbase Premium, which compares Bitcoin’s price on Coinbase with global markets, briefly turned positive at the low as U.S. buyers stepped in.

Still, Glassnode stopped short of calling a bottom. Broad demand remains thin: stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days, and the Coinbase Premium has slipped back to a small discount.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs extended their outflow streak to eight sessions on Monday and have bled about $2.2 billion so far in November, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker.

That makes the $62,000 to $66,000 range the line to watch. Short-term holders bought very few coins below $62,000, and a large cluster of leveraged long positions sits just beneath it, between about $59,500 and $62,200.

A daily close below $62,000 could trigger a fast drop toward the June low of $58,500 and Bitcoin’s realized price of $53,700, the average price at which every coin last moved, Glassnode said.

On the upside, a move back above $74,100, the average cost basis of short-term holders, would confirm that a bottom is forming, according to the firm. Options traders on Deribit, meanwhile, price roughly a one-in-three chance that Bitcoin settles below $53,700 at the September 2027 expiry.

The Fed’s next rate decision is Dec. 9, a day before November inflation data is released.

#4830. 10 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Plus, everything you need to know to find the fragrance that suits your unique style.

FRAGRANCE IS A deeply personal choice. Unlike moisturizers or razors, you don’t have to worry about skin type or sensitivity—cologne is all about preference. For me, I lean woody and amber year-round; however, I’ll branch out to fresher scents during the summer and spring. Whether you’ve worn the same scent for years or switch it up like socks, there’s no shortage of options to explore.

I’ve long been obsessed with Tom Ford’s bold, sophisticated Fucking Fabulous scent, so when I heard a higher-concentrated parfum was dropping earlier this year, I was stoked. It didn’t disappoint either, more than earning its name. Like the original, it layers rich tobacco and warm tonka bean into a scent that’s decadent, intoxicating, and impossible to forget. This new version amps up the intensity and staying power without ever crossing into overpowering territory.

I love how this scent hits—deep leather and roasted tonka wrapped in warm balsamic depth. The first spray bursts with fresh clary sage and lavender before melting into creamy almond and earthy orris. As it settles, the leather gets bolder, stitched with cashmere for a smooth finish. It’s unapologetic, addictive, and every bit as bold as its name. It could also double as the longest-lasting fragrance on this list.

This scent lingers for a long time, even by parfum standards. I’ve had days where I give myself a couple of sprays before leaving my apartment in the morning around 7 AM, and I can still smell it when I get home close to 7 PM. That’s nearly 12 hours of staying power.

Margiela’s Replica fragrances are designed to capture a vibe, and this one is no exception. The infusion of oud wood, leather, smoke, and crackling black pepper instantly transports you to sitting around a crackling fire, the sky ablaze with stars above you. It’s deep and layered, the type of cologne that invites people to get closer to you, and the inclusion of oud adds an air of masculine sophistication that makes it an ideal date night cologne. Compared to other oud-forward scents, this one is both identifiable as oud (i.e., elegant and sexy) but isn’t so overpowering that it’s going to leave a scent trail wherever you go.

A lot is written about Dior Sauvage, and rightfully so—it’s a dark, spicy scent that leaves a serious impression. But much of that hype overshadows the best, most masculine Dior scent: Homme. Dior Homme Parfum takes the classic scent I love and gives it a bolder, woodsy, amber twist that’s built for this chilly weather. The iris at its core feels smooth and modern—soft yet strong—balanced by warm, ambery woods that linger long after the first spray. It hits harder and lasts longer than the original Homme without losing that signature sophistication. Even the bottle reflects its power: sleek, heavy, and designed to look as refined as it smells.

Inspired by a garden after the rain, this new take on freshness leans heavy on the green and skips the citrus, which can overpower its subtle vibe. A hint of juicy pear adds light sweetness and a cooling effect that amplifies it. It also features a note called physcool, which is a chill, minty accord that reacts with the moisture on your skin to create a zingy tingle that drives home the fresh vibe. The result is a modern, versatile scent that works anywhere and on every guy.

I’ve never passed the folks playing chess in Washington Square Park and thought, “Man, I’d love to smell like those dudes.” But the strategy and tension of the game somehow inspired one of my favorite emerging fragrance houses, Mind Games. Its best release to date, Opera Mate, swaps checkmates for curtain calls, channeling the drama of the Paris Opera House into scent form. To me, it smells like a grand finale—elegant, layered, and impossible to ignore.

Opera Mate pulls me in from the first spray with creamy sandalwood and a touch of caramel that melt together into smooth, golden warmth. As it opens, roasted chestnut and grapefruit give it a lift, like a spark before the curtain rises. Then it deepens, revealing rich suede, smoky vetiver, and resinous benzoin that linger on the skin. It feels elegant yet bold, the kind of scent that commands attention without shouting. I wear it when I want to smell like confidence with a touch of drama.

This bottle is a loud, vibrant green reminiscent of Vulcan blood, which is fitting because it’s the logical choice for anyone looking for a refined, interesting scent. The scent itself is amber-woody, sure, but it’s a little spicy and bold without being obnoxious.

It opens with warm, resinous notes of Peru balsam, benzoin, and guaiac wood before evolving into green Bourbon geranium with rosy facets, while bergamot and musk add a fresh lift. It’s a collection of notes that feels like they shouldn’t work, but together create something powerful and new—one of those scents that’s hard to place in a single fragrance family.

When you think of aquatic scents, you typically think of notes like citrus, driftwood, and salty notes that mimic seawater. This surprising cologne, however, flips that idea on its head. Inspired by the Adriatic islands, there are notes of olive oil, fig, pine needles, cypress, and wild herbs. You still have a wet, oceanic quality that gives it an aquatic nature, but without citrus, the effect is earthier and more grounded, not to mention long-lasting and way more sophisticated. If you love fresh colognes but want to elevate your game, this one is for you.

Look, I get why the OG Bleu de Chanel is a classic fragrance; its blend of grapefruit, cedar, and sandalwood hits that sweet spot of being masculine without feeling like it’s begging for attention. But over the past couple of years since Bleu de Chanel L'Exclusif was released—and named a 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award winner—I found myself wearing it far more often.

It’s darker and denser, with much more staying power. The original Bleu de Chanel felt like a crisp summer morning, bright and fresh, whereas L'Exclusif is more like a windy, layered fall evening. It maintains some of the citrusy freshness of the original before evolving into something deeper, with sandalwood, leathery cistus labdanum, and woody amber notes taking over. It’s intense, aromatic, and guaranteed to make a statement.

While I love eating vanilla-flavored things (mostly ice cream, if I’m being honest), I was never a huge fan of the scent. This 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award-winning cologne changed that for me—it’s easily the best vanilla fragrance I’ve worn. Don’t let the name fool you; the vanilla here isn’t the strongest note.

This cologne has a deep, leathery suede base layered with rich labdanum and amber notes for a masculine, cozy scent that’s perfect for cooler weather. The vanilla is just enough to spice things up from my usual leathery or amber colognes, but it doesn’t overpower the core of the fragrance. It’s strong too. A couple of sprays on my neck in the morning lasts me ten hours. Best part? It’s only $82. For a cologne of this quality, you usually have to spend at least twice that.

Read More: 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Awards

I’ve always loved the smell of campfire smoke; the deep, woody burn that clings to your clothes and stays in your memory. City on Fire captures this feeling better than any cologne I’ve ever tried, and I wear it year-round—bold in winter, magnetic in summer. It opens with spicy black pepper and dark berries before revealing layers of cardamom, labdanum, and clearwood that flicker like embers. The scent of cade oil and burnt match adds a rugged, smoldering edge that feels both primal and sophisticated.

Like all Imaginary Authors fragrances, it’s built around a story—in this case, a noir-like tale about two matchmakers drawn together by murder and mystery—and that narrative energy inspires the scent’s smoky, cinematic depth. I love how it lingers for hours, shifting from bright heat to soft ash, like the last glow of a fire you never want to leave. To be clear, this stuff is strong. If you’re not a fan of smoky fragrances, you’ll want to look elsewhere. But if you do dig a smoky cologne, this will quickly become a favorite.

Fragrance families are your roadmap to finding the right cologne. Once you figure out which group you’re drawn to, narrowing your search gets a whole lot easier. The four main families—fresh, floral, woody, and amber—cover almost every scent on the market, though some blends straddle more than one. You might also see fougère listed as a fifth family, but we treat it as a note within the woody category. Here’s how the big four break down:

Be it of the top, heart, or base variety, scent notes are far more specific than fragrance families, often referring to individual scent ingredients or aromas that make up a fragrance. The foundational notes of men’s cologne rarely change, but fragrance chemists (real thing!) are always updating the classics to build younger scents (also a thing!) that smell more modern. Of course, there are many more, but some key notes you’ll find in our favorite colognes are:

The eternal question when faced with purchasing any self-care product is what size to buy. When it comes to cologne, there are a few factors to keep in mind that’ll determine how big or small you’ll want to go here. For one, how often do you plan to wear the cologne? If you plan to make this your new daily scent, buy a bigger bottle so it’ll last longer.

But if you’re merely testing a fragrance or looking for something seasonal, consider a smaller option. Not to mention, cologne can run a bit expensive, especially for some of the stronger versions. So remember that buying a larger container can often offset some of the cost.

Cologne is personal, and what smells incredible on one guy might be missed entirely on another. That’s why the Men’s Health grooming team has been testing and debating scents nonstop since this story first ran in 2020. Over the years, we’ve sprayed, worn, and ranked hundreds of colognes across every fragrance family, taking notes on how they apply, evolve, and hold up through the day.

For this updated guide, I revisited our past favorites, compared them with new releases, and leaned on expert feedback to narrow it all down. Below, you’ll find the ten best colognes for men that are timeless, modern, and made to work in every season.

Apply cologne to the places where you can feel the beats of your heart. This means wrists, the sides of your neck, and over your ticker. The throb adds impact to the scent.

No cologne is perfect for every person, but there are a few best practices to follow when testing a new scent to find the right fit for you. For starters, don't bombard your skin with too many scents. When testing colognes, stick to no more than three on your skin so you can clearly tell each scent apart, says fragrance developer Ann Gottlieb.

So be selective with which you want to trial when browsing in-store because, as Gottlieb warns, testing too many too quickly can lead to nose fatigue. Gottlieb also recommends allowing a scent to linger on you for at least 30 minutes before deciding to buy. This lets you see how a fragrance reacts and develops with your own, unique body chemistry.

#4829. Mel Robbins Started Lifting Weights in Her 50s. Here’s What Her Gym Routine Looks Like

The podcast host breaks it down on the latest episode of Strong Like.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Mel Robbins has always been a mover—running, hiking, skiing, Pilates, yoga, you name it—but it’s only been recently that the 58-year-old has added strength training to her fitness regimen. She credits Dr. Stacy Sims (a Women’s Health advisory board member) and Dr. Vonda Wright, both guests on The Mel Robbins Podcast, with finally persuading her to lift weights.

“They kept saying, when we reach a certain age, 40 and up, for us to start resistance training and with heavier weights,” says Mel, who had to overcome a few fitness myths to finally prioritize pumping iron. “I was nervous I would bulk up. That's a joke, because you know how much you need to train to actually bulk up? I wasn't going to be doing that.”

So what exactly does Mel do in the gym? She walked WH through a typical session for the latest episode of Strong Like.

Before Mel’s feet ever touch a mat, she makes sure to jot down—with actual pen and paper!—what she intends to do at the gym. “This will ensure that you actually do it, because if you're relying on this noggin up here, it ain't happening,” she says.

With her to-do list by her side, Mel begins her session with a warm-up. She runs through a batter of stretches that include inchworms (with an added push-up—go Mel!) and lunges with a twist, before moving on to a banded overhead press to mobilize her shoulders. “I've stopped judging these little bands,” Mel says. “These little suckers look like nothing. Let me tell you, there's a whole lot of something in these bands. You'll be shocked at how much gain you can get and how great this is for you.”

With her warm-up complete, she moves on to the workout, shifting the bands from her arms to her legs for a duck walk. Mimicking the water fowl, she moves forward and back, side to side, keeping outward pressure on the bands.

Next, she tackles one of her favorite moves, a reverse lunge with medicine ball twist. “It's a compound movement that works mobility, your core, your arms, your legs, everything in one movement,” Mel says. “It's super-simple, painful, and awful, and it works like a charm.”

She moves on to the upper body with chest presses, though she has a hack for lighting up even more muscles in the process. “If you want to maximize what you're doing here, suck in your stomach and clench your butt, because then it's not just arms; it's a whole-body thing,” she says.

Finally, she concludes with a snatch, joking: “You can work out a lot of aggression at the world doing [these].”

Ultimately, says Mel, her approach to fitness is pretty straightforward: “I'm not in here because I want to look good in a bathing suit. I do, but that's not the motivation. I'm in here lifting weights because I want to live a long, vibrant, healthy life. I want to be dancing into my late 90s. I want to make sure I can pick up the suitcase and put it up in the overhead. I want to make sure that I am strong so my life is long.”

To hear more about Mel’s gym motivation, click play on the latest episode of Strong Like above!

#4828. Bitcoin drops 2.5% as Nvidia stock risks new 5-month lows into Q3 earnings

Bitcoin price downside sees local lows of $63,269 as Nvidia stock targets $150 as traders brace for volatility over Q3 earnings.

Bitcoin saw selling pressure after Tuesday’s Wall Street open as stock markets stayed on edge ahead of Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings and forward guidance.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD dipping to $63,269 on Bitstamp, down up to 2.5% on the day.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US equities saw minor losses as the session began, with traders eyeing key data from Nvidia, along with cues as to how the company planned to handle the ongoing controversy surrounding its former CEO Jensen Huang.

Amid mounting pressure to reinstate Huang despite resistance from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, commentators saw little chance of Nvidia’s board reversing its decision to dismiss him.

On Tuesday, the board announced the creation of a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, dedicated to “oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.”

“We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” board chairman Harvey Jones commented in a press release.

Huang will also appear to testify before Congress on Dec. 1. In its latest analysis, trading resource The Kobeissi Letter put the odds of Huang returning at less than 20% in light of the latest events.

“Any indication that the probability is higher would be strongly bullish for the stock,” it wrote on X.

Kobeissi queried whether Huang’s departure could justify the $750 billion loss in market cap Nvidia had suffered, with NVDA dipping to $150.35, down over 3% on the day. On Nov. 12, it hit $148.80, its lowest since late June.

Nvidia stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Market nerves extended beyond the US ahead of a key moment for the AI sector. South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI Composite Index finished Tuesday’s trading session 2.6% lower at 4,968 points — its lowest daily close since Feb. 2.

KOSPI one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

“The tape feels increasingly fragile as Nvidia’s AI premium continues to unwind and investors reassess the durability of the ecosystem built around its dominance,” CNBC quoted FedWatch Advisors founder Ben Emons as stating in a note.

CNBC and others referenced data from Bank of America’s latest monthly fund manager survey, which showed that investors slashed tech-stock exposure last month from 37% to 12% overweight tech — the largest single monthly reduction since June 2006.

BTC price action sought to break down from its narrow range between $64,000 and $66,000, in place since Nov. 15, as traders awaited Nvidia signals.

Related: Bitcoin realized loss metric beats June high as open interest eyes 2-year low

In an X update on the day, Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, stipulated that the market needed to fulfil several key conditions as part of a durable rebound.

BTC/USD, he argued, should reclaim its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) at $67,977, but that this alone was not “enough.” Lower time frames must also produce a series of higher swing lows and higher swing highs, with breakouts through local resistance accompanied by high buyer volume.

“Until then, a bounce has a higher probability of being a trap than a legit recovery effort,” Alan summarized.
